title: V & S Teeter Toddlers celebrates 2 years, searching for more staff - WGEM
content: QUINCY (WGEM) -V & S Teeter Toddlers Daycare celebrated two years in business on Friday and is looking towards the future. The daycare has been working towards offering overnight services, but said they still need more staff for that to be possible. “We are in need of more employees, that’s where we’re having trouble,” Shalana Crider, the daughter of a Teeter Toddlers co-owner, said. “If we can get some teachers to come in or even if you want to be a teacher’s aid and we can work on you to be a teacher within three months that would be really appreciated, but it’s grown a lot, but like I said we can’t really open the hours like we want to until we get more employees.” Zariah Lumpkins, teacher assistant, said the biggest goal for the next year is to get their night shift open and make daycare available for families who work evenings or overnights. “Childcare is in high demand,” Lumpkins said. “A lot of people have kids and have jobs and it’s very hard to find reliable childcare outside of centers and schools and all of that.” Lumpkins said it’s been exciting to see the business grow over the last two years and she’s excited for new faces to join the team. To apply, visit the daycare at 3700 E. Lake Center Dr.

title: Norway's King Harald V dies at 89, Haakon VIII succeeds to the throne - China Daily
content: OSLO — Norway's King Harald V died at the age of 89 early on Friday, the Royal House of Norway said. The king passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet at 6:35 am, according to a statement issued by the Royal House. Under Norway's rules of succession, 53-year-old Crown Prince Haakon immediately succeeded to the throne and became the country's new king. The new monarch has taken the name King Haakon VIII, the royal palace said in a post on Instagram on Friday. The new king has chosen the personal motto "Everything for Norway", in keeping with the motto picked by his father, grandfather and great-grandfather since Norway's modern-day monarchy was established in 1905. Harald was admitted to the hospital on Aug 17. The Royal House previously said he had received cortisone treatment for hemolytic anemia in recent weeks, which caused fluid accumulation. During his hospitalization, he was also treated with antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his blood. The Royal House said on Thursday that Harald's health had deteriorated and his condition was "very serious". Born on Feb 21, 1937, Harald ascended to the throne on Jan 17, 1991, following the death of his father, King Olav V. He had been hospitalized several times in recent years and received a permanent pacemaker in 2024. Haakon was born on July 20, 1973. He had served as regent on multiple occasions when his father was ill or abroad. Haakon's eldest child, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, is now Norway's crown princess and the heir to the throne. Harald was Europe's oldest monarch. The king modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who have abdicated in recent times. Like other royal houses in Europe, the Norwegian monarchs serve a largely symbolic role, enjoying celebrity status while real power rests with an elected parliament. "A whole nation is in mourning and the people of Norway are left with a deep sense of gratitude for a long life in the service of Norway," Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said in a statement. "For more than three decades as monarch, Harald V demonstrated an unwavering faith in the Norwegian people. He helped us to see the best in ourselves — and in one another." Harald was 3 years old when the Nazis occupied Norway at the start of World War II. To avoid capture, his mother fled with him and his sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, first to Sweden and then by boat to the US, while Harald's father and grandfather went into exile in Britain with Norway's government. The family was reunited in Norway in June 1945, shortly after the end of the war in Europe. A large crowd gathered outside the palace in Oslo on Thursday, holding their breath for Harald's health, with many staying late into the night, laying flowers and spontaneously singing the national anthem. Kaspara Bolstad, 24, told AFP Harald had been "a very steady and warm king". Other European monarchs have paid tribute to Harald. The kings of Denmark and Sweden called him an "extraordinary" leader and good friend who unified his country. Belgium's King Philippe and Queen Mathilde on Friday expressed their "great sadness", saying his "humor, humanity and sincerity made him a truly special man". The United Kingdom's King Charles III mourned the loss of his "dear cousin" King Harald, paying tribute to a "towering figure" who guided his country with "warmth and humility". The two men were second cousins once removed, both being descendants of Britain's King Edward VII. Copyright 1994 - 2026. All rights reserved. title: In Memory of H.M. King Harald V of Norway - orc.org
content: 28 August 2026 - ORC joins Norway and the sailing world in mourning the loss of H.M. King Harald V, who served for decades as Honorary Chairman of our organization, following many years in the same role at World Sailing, then known as IYRU. He inherited his passion for sailing from his father, King Olav, and after competing in several Olympic Games, moved on to offshore racing in the IOR era, then IMS. His long line of "Fram" yachts was always at the forefront of development. In 1987 he won the One Ton Cup in Kiel aboard a new Farr design (Fram X), before moving on to the ILC40 class, then the 50-footer, with which he won the European ORC Championship in 2005; then the TP52, and finally the Swan 50. His sailing career came full circle in the classic 8- and 6-Metre yachts once raced by his father, where he achieved excellent results as recently as three years ago. His crew was always an example of seamanship as well as camaraderie at major events around the world — often racing against other royalty and high-profile professional crews, yet always with a friendly approach and quiet Norwegian pride. Thomas Nilsson, ORC Mancom, who sailed with the Fram crew for nearly 20 years, adds: "Personally, having had the privilege of being part of that crew for nearly 20 years, I can say that King Harald was, above all, a wonderful team leader — generous, down-to-earth, and endlessly passionate about the sport we shared. Sailing with him was never about titles; it was about the wind, the water, and the people around him. His example won't be forgotten. Fair winds, King." title: 2029 Lotus Esprit to Offer V-6 Option Alongside Hybrid V-8, CEO Confirms - Car and Driver

We already knew about the nearly 1000-hp hybrid V-8 Lotus is planning, but a new report suggests it’ll be paired with a V-6 option. Few founders have left such a strong mark on their company that their ethos remains the driving force of the company even decades after their death, but if such a list exists, Colin Chapman can certainly be counted among its ranks. In the spirit of building lightweight cars—something Chapman famously approved of—Lotus will add a V-6 option to its upcoming Esprit, internally known as Type 135, the brand’s CEO said during a recent earnings call, Autocar reported. The hybrid V-6 option will allow Lotus to comply with tightening global emissions regulations, “while preserving essential Lotus DNA of lightweight engineering and extreme track-focused driving dynamics,” Feng Qingfeng, the brand’s CEO, said during a recent investor relations call. It will join the previously confirmed V-8 hybrid that Lotus is planning for the new flagship model. In the Emira’s case, the powertrain is reportedly good for up to 536 horsepower and 516 pound-feet of torque, though we wouldn’t be shocked to see larger figures for the Esprit. Like the hybrid V-8, the new V-6 is being produced by Horse, the joint venture company owned by Renault and Lotus's parent company, Geely. The larger engine is poised to produce a combined output of at least 986 horsepower and will pair with an eight-speed dual-clutch gearbox. And, despite its higher cylinder count, Lotus is putting considerable effort into keeping the powertrain’s weight down. The Type 135 was originally planned as an electric successor to the Emira before changing market conditions forced Lotus to alter its plans. The full reveal and start of production for the revived Esprit are both planned for 2028. Norway is mourning King Harald V after the monarch died aged 89 at Oslo University Hospital’s Rikshospitalet at 6:35 a.m. local time on Friday, according to the Royal Palace. Hundreds of people gathered outside the palace to lay flowers and wreaths, while church bells rang across the country at noon. The Norwegian Royal Standard was flown at half-mast as officials and members of the public paid tribute to a king who had reigned for more than three decades. Harald became king in January 1991 following the death of his father, King Olav V. His reign spanned a period of strong economic growth, fuelled in large part by Norway’s oil and gas industry. Known for his modern and modest approach to the monarchy, Harald remained a widely respected national figure as the country’s head of state. Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has succeeded his father as King Haakon VIII. He has adopted the motto “All for Norway” (Alt for Norge), the same words used by his great-grandfather, King Haakon VII. Norway’s monarchy is largely ceremonial, with political power resting with the country’s elected parliament. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre signed the book of condolences at the Royal Palace, saying the country had been left with “a deep sense of gratitude” for Harald’s long service.

title: King Frederik and Queen Mary order poignant palace tribute following King Harald V’s death - HOLA
content: King Frederik X and Queen Mary of Denmark ordered a poignant tribute following the death of King Harald V of Norway. The Danish Royal House announced that the national flag was lowered to half-mast at Amalienborg Palace on Friday, August 28, in memory of the late Norwegian monarch, who died peacefully at Oslo University Hospital earlier that morning. He was 89. The solemn image offered a visible reflection of the grief being felt by Denmark’s royal family, whose relationship with Harald extended far beyond their official roles. Frederik and Mary addressed Harald’s son and successor, King Haakon VIII, in a deeply personal message following the news. “Dear Haakon,” their letter began. The couple sent their warmest thoughts and condolences to “Aunt Sonja,” Haakon, his wife, Mette-Marit, and the rest of the Norwegian royal family. “Your father meant a great deal to my mother and both of us,” they wrote, referring affectionately to the late monarch as “Uncle Harald.” Frederik and Mary remembered Harald for his warm and dry sense of humor, unwavering calm and ability to make others feel at ease. They described him as “an extraordinary man, with a twinkle in his eye and a big heart.” “For 35 years, King Harald was a strong unifying figure for the Norwegian people,” their message continued. “He joined duty and responsibility with presence and compassion. He was cherished like few others, and he will be missed by many.” The Danish royals also reflected on the ties between their two countries and families, writing that the Danish-Norwegian bonds remained strong after generations of close connections. The tribute at Amalienborg was one of several visible signs of mourning seen at royal residences across Europe. In the United Kingdom, the Union Flag was lowered to half-mast at Buckingham Palace following the announcement of Harald’s death. Flags were also lowered at Windsor Castle, Clarence House and the Palace of Holyroodhouse in Edinburgh. King Charles III paid tribute to his “dear cousin,” remembering him as a beloved relative and friend who served Norway with “unwavering dedication.” “For thirty-five years, King Harald served his people with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility,” Charles wrote. The British monarch also emphasized the close historical and family ties shared by the United Kingdom and Norway, which were strengthened during World War II. “The Queen and I extend our deepest and most heartfelt condolences to Queen Sonja and all her family,” Charles concluded, adding that Britain shared in Norway’s grief at a time of “heartbreaking loss.” Flags were also lowered at the Royal Palace in Stockholm and at Sweden’s other royal palaces and buildings. The gesture was set to continue on Friday and Saturday, as well as on the day of Harald’s funeral. King Carl XVI Gustaf said that Sweden’s royal family had received the news of their “dear friend” Harald’s death with great sadness. The Swedish government also ordered flags at its offices to be lowered until sunset, describing the Norwegian King as a dependable, respected and unifying figure across both Norway and the Nordic region. In Norway, the government declared an official period of national mourning beginning on the day of Harald’s death and continuing until after his funeral. Flags will remain at half-mast at royal residences, government buildings and military bases throughout the mourning period. Church bells rang across the country following the announcement and will ring again on the day of the funeral. Members of the public gathered outside the Royal Palace in Oslo to lay flowers, light candles and remember the late King. Harald will lie in state in the Palace Chapel before his funeral at Oslo Cathedral, with the date yet to be confirmed. King Harald ascended the throne in 1991 following the death of his father, King Olav V. After 35 years as Norway’s monarch, he has been succeeded by his son, King Haakon VIII. © ¡HOLA! European monarchs and world leaders paid tribute to Norway's King Harald on Friday, after the royal palace announced his death at the age of 89. Harald was the continent's oldest reigning monarch. His son Haakon automatically succeeded him to the throne. Here are some of the main tributes from across the continent and further afield. The kings of Denmark and Sweden called Harald an "extraordinary" leader and good friend who unified his country. "Both as head of state and a successful athlete, he was an outstanding representative of his country. He gave 'All for Norway'," Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf said, referring to Harald's royal motto. Denmark's King Frederik X said the late monarch was "an extraordinary man" who "joined duty and responsibility with presence and compassion." The Dutch royal family recalled "unforgettable" journeys with King Harald around Oslo and the rest of Norway. "We cherish the memory of our special friendship with him in our hearts. King Harald served his country with love, pride, and conviction," the family said in a statement. Harald's "humour, humanity and sincerity made him a truly special man," Belgium's King Philippe and Queen Mathilde said. "Generations of Norwegians grew up with him. For decades, he was a familiar and reassuring presence, a beacon of stability for his country. He fulfilled his role with unwavering dedication, loyalty and dignity," they said in a statement. Spain's royal family hailed King Harald as an "example of responsibility, dignity, simplicity, and tireless dedication to the service" of his country. "With respect and admiration for him, as well as deep sadness, we offer our condolences" on the king's death, they wrote on social media. Britain's King Charles III hailed a "dear cousin" who he said had served "with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility." "As Norway mourns the loss of so towering a figure, my whole family join in remembering a much-loved kinsman and friend whose kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades," the king said in a statement, personally signed Charles R. Harald "worked tirelessly throughout his reign to strengthen the ties uniting Norway and France," Emmanuel Macron wrote on X, recalling a "warm welcome" on his visit to Oslo in June 2025. "His Majesty embodied dignity, wisdom, and an unwavering commitment to his country," said Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a statement. "Ukraine will always remember his steadfast support and solidarity with the Ukrainian people during the darkest days of Russia's aggression." Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, in a post on X, called Harald: "A monarch who served his nation with equanimity, authority and a deep sense of institutional duty, helping to strengthen the ties between Norway and Italy throughout his long reign." The Swiss president Guy Parmelin wrote in a post on X that Harald "will be remembered for his steadfast leadership and devoted service to his country". "Canada mourns with you," said a statement from Mark Carney, offering the condolences of his government. "I had the privilege of meeting his Majesty last March in Olso and he spoke of the ties between our nations with great warmth and affection." Harald "showed himself to be a dedicated leader," posted Mark Rutte, head of the NATO alliance that includes Norway. "His own military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO," he wrote online. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that Harald "served his country with warmth, humility and an unwavering sense of duty." A spokesman for UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply saddened" by the king's death. "He will be remembered for his engagement for children's welfare and environmental issues, his support for diversity and calls for generosity," the statement added. Jordan's Royal Hashemite Court said it mourned the passing of King Harald "may his soul rest in peace." The court "expresses the deepest sympathies of His Majesty and the Jordanian people, as they stand with Norway and its people at this difficult time." King Abdullah ordered his court to observe three days of mourning, a statement from the court added.

title: King Harald V dies after more than three decades on Norway's throne - KSNV
content: King Harald V, a monarch whose personal choices helped redefine a royal family once bound tightly to tradition, died on Friday.  He was 89 years old. Harald died at the National Hospital in Oslo at 6:35 a.m., the palace said. His son, Crown Prince Haakon, immediately succeeded him as King Haakon VIII. FILE - Norway's King Harald arrives at a central London hotel for a pre-royal wedding dinner hosted by Lady Elizabeth Anson and attended by members of the British royal family and foreign royal families, in London, on April, 28, 2011. (AP Photo/Alastair Grant, File) Harald’s life intersected with some of the most consequential moments in modern Norwegian history. He was 3 when Nazi Germany occupied Norway in 1940, forcing the royal family to leave the country. He spent part of the war in the U.S., separated from a homeland that would later look to him as a symbol of continuity. Decades later, his decision to marry Sonja Haraldsen became another defining chapter. Harald met Sonja, then a commoner, in 1959. Their relationship initially faced resistance because she did not come from an aristocratic family. He reportedly made clear to his father that he would not marry anyone else. Their 1968 wedding was seen as a turning point for Norway’s monarchy. OSLO, NORWAY - AUGUST 28: The hearse carrying the coffin of King Harald V of Norway escorted by members of the royal family arrives at Parkveien on August 28, 2026 in Oslo, Norway. The Norwegian palace confirmed that King Harald V passed away at Oslo University Hospital early Friday morning, August 28. (Photo by Rune Hellestad/Getty Images) Harald became king in 1991 after the death of his father, King Olav V. Over more than three decades, he paired the ceremonial duties of the crown with a comparatively informal public style that resonated with many Norwegians. An enthusiastic sailor, Harald competed for Norway in three Olympic Games before ascending the throne. In later years, he faced repeated health challenges and relied increasingly on Haakon to perform official duties. Still, the king remained a familiar national figure, particularly in moments of mourning and crisis. He is survived by Queen Sonja, King Haakon VIII, Princess Märtha Louise, as well as his grandchildren. EDITOR'S NOTE: The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Her eldest son, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted of rape in June and is currently serving a four-year prison sentence. The two scandals have taken a toll on the monarchy, even as the new queen publicly apologized three times. Support for the crown among Norwegians has fallen by roughly 10 percentage points over the past year, while a February poll found that 44 percent believed she should not become queen. She has never been accused of a crime, and nothing in the released files alleges that she took part in Epstein's abuse. Newsweek reached out to the Royal House of Norway, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre's office and the Norwegian Embassy in the U.S. by email for comment. The Royal House announced Harald's death in a statement Friday morning. "It is with deep grief that we announce that His Majesty King Harald has passed away," the statement said. "King Harald died peacefully at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet Friday 28 August at 6:35 AM." Harald had been hospitalized the previous week and was being treated for haemolytic anaemia, a condition in which the body destroys its own red blood cells. On Sunday, the palace said his health had "deteriorated over the weekend" and that he was "receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his blood." His condition was later described as extremely serious. Haakon served as regent during his father's final illness. Harald struggled with health problems for years. He used crutches, had a pacemaker fitted and underwent heart-valve and bladder-cancer surgeries in the early 2000s. He was also hospitalized several times for infections. In February 2024, while on a private holiday on the Malaysian island of Langkawi for his 87th birthday, Harald fell ill and had a temporary pacemaker implanted at a local hospital because of a low heart rate. He was flown back to Norway on a medical evacuation aircraft. He was hospitalized again in Tenerife in February 2026 with an infection and dehydration. "I stick by what I've always said, that I swore an oath to the Storting and it is for life," he said in January 2024, weeks after Denmark's Queen Margrethe II abdicated. Haakon VIII is 53. Born at the National Hospital in Oslo on July 20, 1973, he is Norway's fourth monarch since the country gained full independence from Sweden in 1905. He is named for his great-grandfather, Haakon VII. Unlike his father and grandfather, who attended Oxford, Haakon studied political science at the University of California, Berkeley, graduating in 1999. He earned a master's degree in development studies from the London School of Economics in 2003. He also graduated from the Royal Norwegian Naval Academy in Bergen in 1995 and completed the Foreign Ministry's diplomat trainee program. From 2020 onward, Haakon served as regent whenever his father was ill, which became increasingly frequent in Harald's final years. Haakon married Mette-Marit, a commoner and single mother, at Oslo Cathedral on August 25, 2001, despite considerable public opposition. Their daughter, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, was born in January 2004 and becomes crown princess and heir apparent at 22 under the absolute primogeniture rules Norway adopted in 1990. Their son, Prince Sverre Magnus, was born in 2005. The new queen's contact with Epstein became public in December 2019, three months after the sex offender's death, when she told the Norwegian business daily Dagens Næringsliv that she had met him several times. "I never would have associated with Mr. Epstein if I had been aware of the seriousness of the crimes he committed," she said in a statement released through the palace on December 2, 2019. "I should have investigated his past more thoroughly, and I am sorry that I didn't." The palace said then that she had cut off contact with him in 2013. The documents released this year painted a more damaging picture. Norwegian outlets NRK, VG and Dagbladet reported that her correspondence with Epstein continued from 2011 into 2014 and that she stayed at his Palm Beach, Florida, mansion for four days in 2013. The Royal House said that the visit was arranged through a mutual friend. The emails drew particular attention. In October 2011, three years after Epstein pleaded guilty in Florida to procuring a minor for prostitution, she wrote that she had Googled him and that it "didn't look too good," followed by a smiley face. In 2012, after Epstein said he was in Paris "on a wife hunt," she replied that the city was "good for adultery" and that "Scandis [are] better wife material." She called him "such sweetheart" and signed one message "Love, Mm." In June 2014, Epstein asked whether he would see her in New York. "Tuesday will work," she replied, contradicting the palace's claim that contact had ended in 2013. She issued another statement through the palace on January 31, a day after the DOJ released the documents: "I showed poor judgment and regret having had any contact with Epstein at all," she said. "It is simply embarrassing." On February 6, she apologized again to the public and the royal family. In a 20-minute NRK interview on March 20, recorded at Skaugum, she said she had been "manipulated and deceived" and did not know Epstein was a sex offender. She said she saw him only with adults and recalled feeling unsafe on the final day of her Palm Beach visit. She called Haakon's residence that day, a call he confirmed that he remembered. She described the "wife hunt" exchange as banter and said Epstein's behavior was sleazy. Støre said that she had shown poor judgment and called on her to explain herself. On February 10, the Norwegian parliament Storting's scrutiny committee voted to open an independent inquiry into Epstein's connections in Norway. The investigation also involves former Prime Minister Thorbjørn Jagland, Terje Rød-Larsen and diplomat Mona Juul. Økokrim, Norway's special police unit and public prosecutor office, has separately opened a corruption investigation into Jagland. Støre said the entire nation was in mourning. The U.K.'s King Charles III described Harald as a "friend whose kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades." Norway has declared a period of national mourning. Flags will fly at half-staff, and church bells will ring across the country. Haakon will formally inform the Cabinet of his father's death at an extraordinary Council of State before swearing a constitutional oath before the Storting. There will be no coronation because Norway abolished the ceremony in 1908. Harald's funeral will be at Oslo Cathedral, and he will be buried in the royal mausoleum at Akershus Fortress alongside his father, Olav V. Haakon is taking the throne as the monarchy faces declining public support. The Storting voted 141-26 on February 3 to keep the monarchy, rejecting a proposal to establish a republic. A Verdens Gang survey published the day before the vote found that 61 percent supported the monarchy, down from 72 percent a year earlier. Support for a republic rose 10 points to 27 percent. Mette-Marit's standing has also suffered. Asked whether she should become queen, 44 percent of those surveyed said no, while 33 percent said yes. A Norstat poll put support for the monarchy at a record low of 60 percent in February before it recovered some to 64 percent in May. Haakon has defended his wife as she has faced scrutiny. Asked about her situation in a televised interview in March, he said: "When you get married, it's for better or for worse." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Kate Nalepinski and Dave Siminoff.

title: Why Hardy Bullock’s defense of failed Measure V surprised me (Opinion) - Sierra Sun
content: I attended the Nevada County Board of Supervisors meeting on August 25 and made a specific request during public comment: I asked the Board to direct County staff, with the involvement of Auditor-Controller Gina Will’s office, to determine and publicly disclose the complete taxpayer cost of Measure V. Several hours later, during Board member announcements, Supervisor Hardy Bullock delivered prepared remarks concerning the recent Fair Political Practices Commission enforcement action involving Measure V. Bullock framed his disagreement as his personal view, stating that, “in my view,” the FPPC’s conclusions did not align with constitutional standards. I respect his right to express that opinion. Bullock offered a detailed defense of the Measure V effort, praised the work of County staff and community members, characterized the County’s actions as a good-faith effort to inform voters, and said he “respectfully and entirely” disagreed with the FPPC’s findings. What he did not address was the question I had asked earlier: What did Measure V actually cost Nevada County taxpayers? We know the County spent $34,614 in public funds on two Measure V mailers and has now agreed to a $31,500 administrative penalty. But that is only part of the cost. Measure V had to be conceived, researched, developed, legally reviewed, presented to the Board and placed before voters. County executives, department heads, County Counsel, employees and consultants devoted public resources to that process. Bullock acknowledged the extent of that effort himself, describing Measure V as the product of “extensive work by this board, by senior staff, and by relevant community members.” Precisely. Extensive government work has a taxpayer cost. The expense also continued after voters rejected Measure V. For years, County Counsel, staff, executives and outside attorneys dealt with the FPPC investigation and negotiated its resolution. · How much County Counsel, executive and employee time was consumed? · What was spent on outside attorneys, consultants and contractors? · What did Measure V-related Public Records Act responses cost? · What was the cost of negotiating and resolving the FPPC proceeding before adding the $31,500 penalty? Bullock’s defense is particularly difficult for me to understand in light of what Nevada County itself agreed to. Nevada County entered into a Stipulation, Decision and Order with the FPPC. The County agreed that it committed seven Political Reform Act violations and that the stipulation contained a “true and accurate summary of the facts.” The stipulation states that the first mailer “crossed the line from informational content into advocacy” and, most significantly, that “the County supported the passage of a local measure using $34,614 in public funds.” That isn’t my characterization. It is contained in the stipulated resolution Nevada County agreed to, signed on its behalf by current Board Chair Lisa Swarthout. Swarthout, however, was not a supervisor when Measure V was placed on the ballot. District 3 was then represented by Dan Miller. On August 9, 2022, the Board voted 4–1 to place Measure V before voters. Heidi Hall, Ed Scofield, Sue Hoek and Hardy Bullock voted yes. Miller voted no. Swarthout was elected later that November and took office in January 2023. Bullock was therefore part of the Board majority that placed Measure V on the ballot. Four years later, after Nevada County entered into the stipulated FPPC resolution, Bullock publicly stated that he “respectfully and entirely” disagreed with the FPPC’s findings. · Does he believe the County should not have entered the settlement? · Does he dispute that the mailers crossed the line into advocacy? · Does he believe Nevada County agreed to violations it did not commit? To Bullock’s credit, he acknowledged that voters rejected Measure V and said he respected their decision. Measure V received 48.41% support and failed. But taxpayers still don’t know what the entire undertaking cost. I believe that if the complete record ultimately establishes that particular individuals were responsible for improper expenditures of taxpayer resources, there should be individual accountability to whatever extent the law provides. Accountability, however, should follow evidence—and the first step is a complete accounting. Government employee time doesn’t become free simply because no separate check was written for every hour. Bullock is entitled to believe the Measure V effort was undertaken in good faith and to disagree with the FPPC. But good intentions do not erase stipulated facts, and disagreement does not pay the bill. Before Nevada County closes the book on Measure V, the Board should direct County staff, with the involvement of Auditor-Controller Gina Will’s office, to answer one simple question: What did failed Measure V actually cost Nevada County taxpayers? Michael Taylor is a Nevada County native, writer, and civic policy advocate focused on government accountability, transparency, and bipartisan reform. A moderate independent who once leaned left, he now finds his views more aligned with constitutionally based libertarian principles. title: Tottenham v Newcastle United: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: Big-spending Tottenham host a Newcastle side that boast an excellent recent record against the north Londoners. BBC Sport takes a look at some of the key themes.. After making such a shocking start to the season against Brentford last Saturday, Tottenham's 5-1 victory against Charlton in the League Cup at least provided a much-needed fillip. The manner of Spurs' insipid defeat at the Gtech Community Stadium was as bad as anything seen under Thomas Frank or Igor Tudor last season and was of great worry to boss Roberto de Zerbi and fans alike. Brentford had an xG of 3.87, six big chances and their 26 shots was the most Spurs had faced in 142 Premier League fixtures dating all the way back until October 2022. The Lilywhites have accrued just 79 points from their last 77 Premier League matches since the start of the 2024-25 campaign, a tally that is under half Arsenal's total of 162 across the same period. Just 36 of those points have come at home and surely top of De Zerbi's to-do list this season will be getting the club back to winning ways in front of their own supporters. The north Londoners have a poor recent record against the Geordies with only one win in eight league encounters (D1, L6) and no clean sheet in 14. Not only that, but Newcastle's tally of 13 away wins at Spurs in the Premier League is more than they've recorded against any other club. One thing that has been guaranteed in meetings between these sides is goals. It is the most played fixture in Premier League history to never end 0-0, with at least one goal scored in all 62 of their meetings. Fans were thrilled with the cameo by new recruit Savio against Charlton as he notched a goal and an assist on his debut. At £75m (rising to £85m with add ons), he's remarkably only the club's third most expensive signing of this summer alone following their unprecedented splurge in the transfer market. But other than netting nine times for Girona in 2023-24, the Brazilian has never scored more than once in a top-flight season, a figure De Zerbi wants a huge improvement on. "The best wingers score many goals," the Spurs boss says. "I spoke with him: we put the (target) on 10-12 goals because we need 10-12 goals from the wingers." After such a challenging and downbeat summer Newcastle fans were heartened and enthused by their performance against Liverpool under new boss Matthias Jaissle. They put in a display full of pace and attacking endeavour and were only denied three points due to Dominik Szoboszlai's last-minute penalty. At the forefront was player-of-the-match Yoane Wissa. After scoring just one league goal in an injury disrupted first season with the Geordies he had been written off in many quarters, but was superb operating in a new number 10 role. Another player rejuvenated after suffering a tough debut campaign on Tyneside was Anthony Elanga. Having failed to score a Premier League goal, he finally got off the mark last week and it's surely no coincidence that his side played a style of football that wasn't dissimilar to the one he excelled in at Nottingham Forest. And continuing on a theme, Joe Willock scored in the Premier League for the first time since February 2024 to end a run of 61 games and 40 shots without a top-flight goal. One failing from last season that reared its head again was the surrendering of leads. The Magpies took their tally of points dropped from winning positions since the start of last season to a whopping 29.

title: Liverpool v Nottingham Forest: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: Nottingham Forest travel to Liverpool looking to secure a hat-trick of league wins at Anfield for the very first time. BBC Sport looks at the key themes. Andoni Iraola's first Premier League game in charge of Liverpool may have ended on a positive note with their last-gasp equaliser at St James' Park, but it was a 90 minutes that also shone a light on the weaknesses his side currently have. The Reds enjoyed 61% possession and had a whopping 27 shots to Newcastle's 13 but at times they were cut apart with ease by the home side's direct and pacy counter attacks. The Geordies' opening goal from Anthony Elanga came just 10 seconds after Newcastle won the ball in their own box, while their second took just 12 seconds from Malick Thiaw winning possession to Joe Willock finishing past Alisson with aplomb. It raised the tally of goals the Reds have conceded from fast breaks in all competitions since the start of last season to nine, the highest of any Premier League side. Iraola takes charge of his first competitive match at Anfield looking to protect the club's proud record of having not lost their opening league game of the season on home soil since 2003, with 17 wins and five draws from 22 such matches. However, that impressive run will come under threat from a Nottingham Forest side that have got used to winning at Anfield. Having not triumphed there in any competition since 1969 they enjoyed a 1-0 victory in September 2024 before following it up with a thumping 3-0 success last November. In fact, since Forest's return to the top-flight in 2022 their three league wins over Liverpool is more than any other side has managed against the Reds in that time. Like Liverpool, Nottingham Forest are trying to find their feet under a new manager in Oliver Glasner. He will certainly be glad to see the back of Leeds United after Daniel Farke's side inflicted back-to-back defeats on them within four days in which they failed to score a goal. A downbeat Glasner said after Tuesday's League Cup loss that the club have to a long way to go before they get to where he wants them to be. "The reality is, and I think everybody has to understand and accept, nine months of relegation battle, losing maybe your top midfielder (Elliot Anderson), and now we're six weeks together," the former Palace boss said. "The reality is no magician, no Messiah, it's just hard work. This is what we have to do." A quiet summer by their recent standards in the transfer market was reflected by Glasner including no new signings in his starting line-up for their opener last Saturday. However, the arrival of club-record signing Liam Delap will give everyone a lift. The £50m striker will be desperate to reignite his career after scoring just one goal in 28 league games in a frustrating spell at Stamford Bridge. Forest will at least be buoyed by the fact they have scored in each of their last 10 Premier League away games – the longest current run in the top flight - netting 15 goals in their last five on the road alone.

title: King Harald V dies at 89, ending a 35-year reign over Norway - Deseret News
content: King Harald V of Norway, who fled to the United States from the Nazis as a child and was Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, has died at age 89, after 35 years on the throne. Harald was immediately succeeded by his son, King Haakon VIII. Haakon’s eldest child, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, is now heir to the throne. “It is with deep sadness that we announce that His Majesty King Harald passed away today. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University hospital on Friday 28 August at 6.35am,” the Oslo palace said in a statement. The king’s health had deteriorated significantly over the last week after he was admitted to the hospital to be treated over complications with a rare blood disorder, haemolytic anaemia. He later developed an infection and was in “extremely serious” condition, per the BBC. Crowds of mourners gathered outside the royal palace in Oslo to pay their respects, laying flowers and flags at the palace gates. The royal flag on the roof of the palace was lowered to half-staff and a period of national mourning was declared leading up to the funeral. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said he received the news “with great sorrow.” “A whole nation is in mourning and the people of Norway are left with a deep sense of gratitude for a long life in the service of Norway,” Støre continued. “Harald V demonstrated an unwavering faith in the Norwegian people. He helped us to see the best in ourselves — and in one another.” Royalty across Europe also shared their condolences. King Charles III sent his “most heartfelt condolences” to the family of his “dear cousin” — Harald and Charles are second cousins once removed. Charles’ statement continued, “As Norway mourns the loss of so towering a figure, my whole family join in remembering a much-loved kinsman and friend whose kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades.” Carl XVI Gustaf, king of Sweden, wrote, “Throughout the years, King Harald has been a good friend to me, my family, and to Sweden. King Harald is now mourned by many in our ​country.” Spain’s royal household shared their “respect and admiration for his legacy,” adding that he was “an example of responsibility, dignity, humility and tireless dedication to the service of Norway and its people.” And Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde remembered Harald for his “humour, humanity and sincerity,” and said they would “cherish the memory of the moments we shared with him.” Born in 1937, Harald was 3 years old when the Nazis occupied Norway at the start of World War II, forcing him to flee with his mother and sisters to Sweden and later to the U.S. to avoid capture. During their time in the U.S., the royal Norwegian family stayed in Washington, D.C., and were frequent guests at the White House, per NPR. Harald was 8 years old at the end of the German occupation, and his family was reunited in Norway. He later married Sonja Haraldsen in a lavish ceremony at the Oslo Cathedral in August 1968. title: This Indiana Lawsuit Against Planned Parenthood Is Ground Zero for Abortion Rights in Blue States - Slate
content:
Sign up for Executive Dysfunction, a weekly newsletter that highlights one under-the-radar story about how Trump is changing the law—or how the law is pushing back—and keeps you posted on the latest from Slate’s Jurisprudence team. For a time, after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, a civil war between the states on reproductive rights seemed inevitable. Red-state attorneys general threatened out-of-state doctors with criminal charges and lawsuits; blue states responded with shield laws that aimed to protect residents from out-of-state legal consequences. These conflicts appeared to be heading for a reckoning, but then things went quiet. That reckoning, however, is about to come due. Specifically, we should expect things to accelerate quickly after the midterms, when Republicans won’t have to worry that unpopular abortion policies will cost Donald Trump a congressional majority. A major new case shows that the ultimate battleground here may not be over telemedicine abortion but about the freedom of speech. That is the issue at the heart of a major new case called Planned Parenthood Northwest v. Commissioner of the Indiana State Department. The case began when Indiana passed a law in 2017 involving abortion access for minors. Before Roe was overturned, most states applied laws allowing minors to get abortions without parental involvement using a procedure called a judicial bypass. In those hearings, minors could avoid parental involvement requirements if they could show that they were mature enough to make a decision themselves or that an abortion would otherwise be in their best interests. Indiana passed a 2017 law that made it a crime to knowingly or intentionally aid or assist a minor seeking an abortion without getting parental consent or using the bypass procedure, and Planned Parenthood sued, arguing that the law violated the First Amendment. It was clear from the beginning that the case would have national implications. Conservatives across the country have since launched a crackdown on speech about abortion. South Dakota passed a law restricting abortion-related advertising. The attorneys general of Florida and Missouri are seeking hundreds of millions of dollars from Planned Parenthood because the organization points to evidence that the abortion pill mifepristone is safe. When—and whether—red states can criminalize speech about abortion is an issue that is likely to head to the Supreme Court, and the Indiana case—which since the fall of Roe has turned on the question of Planned Parenthood’s informational efforts surrounding out-of-state abortions—may be the reason why. It’s not lost on conservatives that they might be violating the First Amendment, and they have come up with two ways to get around that obstacle. Indiana, for example, argued that speech isn’t protected when it is integral to a crime. The idea is simple: We don’t protect the speech necessary to plan a heist or put out a hit. Indiana insisted that Planned Parenthood’s referrals for out-of-state care fell in the same category. But Planned Parenthood pointed out a key distinction: Robbery and murder are crimes in every state, but in large swaths of the country, abortion is constitutionally protected. That means that Indiana’s law and others like it will force the courts to figure out which state law to apply when a clash arises. The 7th Circuit had to rule on just that question when it came to Indiana’s law. Indiana acknowledged that Planned Parenthood was facilitating legal abortions. What was illegal, the state said, was the speech that took place in Indiana. The court disagreed: It couldn’t be a crime to help someone do something that was legal in the place where it occurs. That conclusion makes sense, but it raises a question that the Supreme Court may have to confront: Which state’s criminal code is the one that counts? Courts here will have to rely on a messy rules governing conflicts of law. The closest thing to a rule of thumb holds that courts should apply the rules of the state that has the most significant relationship to the case. Blue states will have a good argument on that point, as the 7th Circuit recognized: When someone travels to another state for abortion, most of the relevant players and events will be in that jurisdiction. But there is no guarantee the conservative Supreme Court supermajority will see it that way. Red states will argue that both the pregnant patient and her fetus come from within their borders—and that the speech needed to plan an abortion took place there too. Even if conservatives lose on this point, they have a backup plan: arguing that abortion-related speech isn’t speech at all. Courts are sometimes more forgiving of burdens on speech when the real focus of a law is conduct, and when any restriction on speech is minor and incidental. That’s what Indiana said was happening here: Lawmakers were mostly interested in stopping out-of-state travel and abortion, not speech about it. The 7th Circuit didn’t buy it: Indiana’s law applied to doctors who provided information and referrals, and that had everything to do with speech. One of the factors that weighed the most heavily in the court’s decision again was that Indiana was punishing speech about something that was legal and protected in other states. From there, the court had little trouble concluding that Indiana’s law regulated based on the content of Planned Parenthood’s speech—a third rail in free-speech law—and could not satisfy strict scrutiny, the demanding standard applied to that kind of speech regulation. This case is just latest example of federal courts being pulled into interstate conflicts about abortion. So far, judges have generally agreed with the 7th Circuit that red states can’t criminalize speech that facilitates something that blue states protect, but the Supreme Court has so far remained on the sidelines. It is only a matter of time before the cold war between the states on reproductive rights comes to life, and there is no telling what that will mean for the First Amendment. title: King Harald V of Norway Has Died After 35 Years On the Throne. Meet His Successor, Haakon - Time Magazine
content: This website uses cookies to enhance user experience and to analyze performance and traffic on our website. We also share information about your use of our site with our social media, advertising and analytics partners. Follow this section to personalize your feed and get instant alerts. Follow this tag to personalize your feed and get instant alerts. Follow this author to personalize your feed and get instant alerts. The new King and Queen of Norway, Mette-Marit and Haakon, are seen here at the Norwegian Constitution Day in Oslo on May 17, 2026. Follow this author to personalize your feed and get instant alerts. King Harald V of Norway, a reformer and Europe’s oldest monarch, died Friday at the age of 89. His son, the newly-proclaimed King Haakon VIII, has inherited the Norwegian throne. Harald passed away peacefully in his sleep at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet at 6:35 a.m., local time, the Royal Palace of Norway said. “A whole nation is in mourning and the people of Norway are left with a deep sense of gratitude for a long life in the service of Norway,” said Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. “For more than three decades as monarch, Harald V demonstrated an unwavering faith in the Norwegian people. He helped us to see the best in ourselves—and in one another.” Harald had been admitted to the hospital on Aug. 17 and placed on sick leave after corticosteroid treatment for haemolytic anemia caused fluid retention that required hospital care, the palace revealed. His son, then-Crown Prince Haakon, 53, served as regent while his father was on leave. In an update on Aug. 23, the palace announced the King’s condition had worsened and that he would remain in the hospital to receive antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream. In recent days, Norwegians had begun to lay flowers in front of the palace in Oslo after the royal household said his condition had become “very serious.” Harald has been described as a monarch who modernized the institution. His marriage broke with royal convention when he wed the non-royal Sonja Haraldsen in 1968 after a lengthy struggle for permission from his family. In a widely noted 2016 Palace garden speech, Harald defined Norwegianness as encompassing immigrants, people of different religions, and members of the LGBTQ+ community. While Norway is a constitutional monarchy, with the king serving as head of state similar to other royal houses in Europe, Norwegian monarchs have largely held symbolic roles, as legislative power rests with an elected parliament. Stortinget, Norway’s parliament, said Friday that the King’s reign “was marked by closeness to the people” thanks to “the unifying way in which he has exercised his royal duties.” Norway will observe a period of mourning, with flags at royal residences, government buildings, and military installations set to remain at half-mast. Church bells rang out on Friday and thousands of people lined the streets as Harald V's coffin, accompanied by a motorcade of black cars, was transported to the Royal Palace in Oslo. As Norway mourns its long-reigning monarch, thoughts are also turning to his successor, who has been tasked with carrying on his father's legacy. Here’s what to know about what comes next and how King Harald is being remembered by his peers and European leaders. When a monarch in Norway passes away, the next person in the order of succession automatically becomes King or Queen, as the country cannot be without a head of state. While succession was previously restricted to male heirs, since 1990 the Constitution was amended so female and male children would be included on an equal footing in the order of succession. However, for those born before the change, a male child retains precedence over an older female sibling. As such, although Princess Märtha Louise was Harald’s eldest child, the crown automatically passed down to his son, Haakon. King Haakon VIII’s wife, Mette-Marit Tjessem Høiby, is the new Queen of Norway. The late King Harald's wife, Queen Sonja, will also retain her title. Haakon and Mette-Marit's daughter Ingrid Alexandra is now Crown Princess and heir apparent—the next person in line to the throne. The Norwegian government convened for an extraordinary cabinet meeting at the palace on Friday at 11:30 a.m., local time, where ministers met the new King. Haakon announced his royal motto, opting to keep the words used by his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather: "All for Norway." There will be no formal coronation for Haakon as Norway’s parliament removed the constitutional requirement for coronations in 1908, deeming the ceremony to be undemocratic and outdated. As the only son of Harald and Sonja, Haakon somewhat broke with tradition in his younger years when he moved out of the country to attend the University of California, Berkeley, where he obtained a BA in political science in 1999. Haakon wed Mette-Marit in 2001, a non-royal and single mother of Marius Borg Høiby. The couple welcomed their first child together, Ingrid Alexandra, in 2004 and had their son, Sverre Magnus, a year later. Marius Borg Høiby, Mette-Marit’s eldest child, was found guilty of two counts of rape and was sentenced to four years in prison in June. In recent years, Mette-Marit has suffered with poor health, after being diagnosed with a chronic lung disease—what the palace referred to as an “unusual variant of fibrosis”—in 2018. In July, Mette-Marit shared a statement upon being discharged from hospital after undergoing a lung transplant. “It has given me the gift of life, and words fall short when I try to describe how grateful and humble I am for this,” she said of the surgery. Mette-Marit has come under scrutiny over her contact with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Files released by the Justice Department in January showed she had maintained correspondence with Epstein in the years after he pled guilty on two counts of soliciting prostitution from a minor in 2008. “Jeffrey Epstein is personally responsible for his actions. I must take responsibility for not checking Epstein’s background more thoroughly and for not understanding quickly enough what kind of person he was,” Mette-Marit said in a statement on Jan. 30 2026. “I deeply regret that, and this is a responsibility I must take. I showed poor judgment and regret ever having had any contact with Epstein. It is simply embarrassing. I want to express my deep sympathy and solidarity with the victims of the abuses committed by Jeffrey Epstein.” During a TV interview in March, Mette-Marit, while sitting beside her husband Haakon, said she wished she had never met Epstein and again expressed regret over the contact. Her Majesty Queen Sonja of Norway and His Majesty King Harald of Norway attend a Norwegian Constitution Day event at the Royal Palace in Oslo, Norway, on May 17, 2026. Ole Hagen––Getty Images Tributes have poured in from around the world to honor the late King and his legacy. Britain’s King Charles III, who is a cousin of Harald, said he and his wife, Queen Camilla, had learned of the news with “the most profound sadness.” “For thirty-five years, King Harald served his people with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility,” Charles said. “As Norway mourns the loss of so towering a figure, my whole family join in remembering a much-loved kinsman and friend whose kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades.” Spain’s monarchy said Harald was “an example of responsibility, dignity, simplicity, and tireless dedication to the service of Norway and its people, before and during his 35 years of reign.” NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte described the late King as a “dedicated leader,” whose “military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO.” Harald's military roots go back to when he attended the Norwegian Military Academy in Oslo as a young royal and went on to be appointed general and admiral in 1977, as part of the royal tradition where the Crown Prince is appointed to the highest rank in the branches of defense at the age of 40. Senior officials within the European Union also offered their condolences, with Norway serving as a close trading and security partner of the bloc. E.U. foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Harald was “truly the people’s King, a lifelong defender of freedom and champion of an open Norwegian democracy and society.” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said the late King had brought Norwegians together “in moments of joy and sorrow.” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz lamented that Norway had lost “a great personality who stood for composure and unity,” while French President Emmanuel Macron said Harald had “worked tirelessly throughout his reign to strengthen the bonds uniting Norway and France.” Norwegian soccer player Erling Haaland, who met with the late King in July after returning from the World Cup 2026, said: “Rest in peace, King Harald. Thank you for everything you meant to Norway. It was an honor to meet you." © 2026 TIME USA, LLC. All Rights Reserved. title: St. Olaf mourns passing of King Harald V of Norway - St. Olaf College
content: St. Olaf College, which was founded by Norwegian immigrants and has maintained deep and enduring ties to Norway, is mourning the death of His Majesty King Harald V. He died on August 28 in Oslo at age 89. “We extend our deepest condolences to Queen Sonja, the Royal Family, and the people of Norway,” says St. Olaf President Susan Rundell Singer. “Generations of Norwegian immigrants and their descendants shaped our college and campus community. King Harald understood the importance of this connection and heritage while also embracing a shared sense of responsibility for the future.” Over the decades, King Harald V visited St. Olaf on three separate occasions. He first visited the college as Crown Prince in 1965. After acceding to the throne, he returned to campus in 1995 alongside Queen Sonja of Norway and was awarded an honorary doctorate. Their Majesties King Harald V and Queen Sonja of Norway visited St. Olaf again in 2011 as part of their official state visit to the United States. While on campus, Their Majesties toured the recently opened Tomson Hall, visited a Norwegian language class, and attended a Sammenkomst (gathering) held in their honor. “One of the most touching photos of that visit is of His Majesty sitting in a desk in that Norwegian class, laughing heartily alongside our students. It underscored his appreciation for education and joy at the way the Norwegians who founded St. Olaf created a lasting appreciation for his country’s culture, language, and values. We will honor his memory by continuing to do this work,” Rundell Singer says. “One of the most touching photos of that visit is of His Majesty sitting in a desk in that Norwegian class, laughing heartily alongside our students. It underscored his appreciation for education and joy at the way the Norwegians who founded St. Olaf created a lasting appreciation for his country’s culture, language, and values. We will honor his memory by continuing to do this work.” Professor of Norwegian and King Olav V Chair in Scandinavian-American Studies Kari Lie Dorer — who was teaching the class photographed during that visit — notes that in addition to visiting classes, King Harald has been a meaningful part of the college’s curriculum. “I strive to do more than teach a language as a subject of study; I want students to understand the true value of a culture, its history, and how those elements have shaped a uniquely progressive society. One way the Norwegian Department does this is by integrating King Harald’s annual New Year’s Eve speeches, which set the tone for Norwegian social values from the top down,” she says. “This in itself is a culture shock for many American students, who are accustomed to political addresses centered on economics or legislative policy rather than human well-being. Over the years, his speeches have consistently prioritized empathy, mental health, and inclusivity, showing our students a striking contrast in what a nation can expect from its leaders.” His Majesty King Harald V of Norway was born on February 21, 1937. The only son of Crown Prince Olav (the future King Olav V) and Crown Princess Märtha, he acceded to the throne when his father passed away in 1991. Like his father and grandfather, he adopted the motto Alt for Norge (“We give our all for Norway”). He will be succeeded by his son, now known as His Majesty King Haakon VIII, who visited St. Olaf in October 2025 as a part of a weeklong trip to the United States to commemorate the 200th anniversary of organized Norwegian migration to North America. King Haakon VIII has already followed in his father’s footsteps and embraced Alt for Norge. St. Olaf is one of few U.S. higher education institutions where students can study Norwegian to complete their foreign language requirement and also be able to further develop their knowledge of Norwegian language, literature, culture, and history. St. Olaf also hosts the Norwegian-American Historical Association (NAHA) and the office of the Oslo International Summer School (ISS) on campus. In addition to visits by Norwegian royalty, including a trip to campus by Her Majesty Queen Sonja in October 2022, St. Olaf also welcomed Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre to campus in September 2023. “The frequent visits from the Norwegian royal family and parliament offer our students that same tangible connection, transforming classroom lessons into a firsthand experience of modern Norwegian culture,” Lie Dorer says. “Importantly, the impact extends far beyond ancestral pride: as an increasing number of our students come from non-Norwegian backgrounds, this bond offers them a vital lens into global citizenship, progressive governance, and shared human values, affirming both St. Olaf’s heritage and our future.” Director of Editorial and Communications We are grateful for the impact your gifts make possible on the Hill.

title: Darlene V. Hopf, 84, Ireland - Dubois County Free Press, Inc.
content: Darlene V. Hopf, 84, of Ireland, Ind., passed away surrounded by family at 2:20 a.m. on Thursday, August 27, 2026, at Deaconess Memorial Medical Center in Jasper, Indiana. Darlene was born in Jasper, Indiana, on April 25, 1942, to Raymond and Lucille (Morgenroth) Schuetter. She married William J. Hopf on September 17, 1960, at St. Mary Catholic Church in Ireland, Indiana. He preceded her in death on December 25, 2022. She was a 1960 graduate of Ireland High School. She was a cook at the Jasper House and later a fabric cutter at Touch of Class. Most recently, she had been a machine operator for Kimball Electronics, where she worked for over 15 years until her retirement. She was a member of St. Mary Catholic Church in Ireland and the St. Ann’s Society. She was a devout Catholic and was a religious education teacher and Eucharistic Minister for the parish. Darlene enjoyed cooking, sewing, being in nature, gardening, canning, and spending time with family and friends.  She loved the holidays and entertaining for family; she would get everyone together and prepare a wonderful meal. She is survived by two sons, Duane Hopf of Jasper and Darren Hopf of Otwell; two daughters, Cindy (Jimmy Dean) Simpson of Crossville, Tenn. and Christine (Jon) Martin of Indianapolis; seven grandchildren, Craig (Jessica) and Robert (Kayla) Abbott, Alicia (Cody) Elmore, Jon (Anne), Zach, and Mariah Martin, and Janis (Marcus) Monroe; 11 great-grandchildren; one sister, Doris Stemle of Celestine; and two brothers, Ray (Evelyn) Schuetter of Holland and David (Annette) Schuetter of Schnellville; and several nieces and nephews. Preceding her in death, besides her husband, is one brother, Don Schuetter. A Mass of Christian Burial for Darlene V. Hopf will be held at 10:00 a.m. on Thursday, September 3, 2026, at St. Mary Catholic Church in Ireland, Indiana, with burial to follow in the church cemetery. A visitation will be held from 4:00 to 7:00 p.m. on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, at the Becher-Kluesner Downtown Chapel in Jasper, Indiana, and one hour before services at the church on Thursday from 9:00 to 10:00 a.m.  St. Mary Parish will pray a rosary at 3:30 p.m. at the funeral home. Memorial contributions may be made to St. Mary Catholic Church or the Alzheimer’s Association. Online condolences may be made at www.becherkluesner.com.

title: What K.G.M. v. Meta Platforms Means for Liability and Free Speech - R Street Institute
content:
In K.G.M. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., a 20-year-old woman alleged that she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube after prolonged use starting from childhood. She argued that infinite scrolling, autoplay, and algorithmic recommendations are designed to keep young users engaged and that they contribute to serious mental health injuries. Meta and Google were found negligent in the design or operation of Instagram and YouTube, with the jury concluding that both companies failed to provide adequate warnings and awarding $6 million in compensatory and punitive damages. But even if the verdict is ultimately overturned, the theory behind it matters because K.G.M. may provide future plaintiffs a legal path around such cases’ traditional focus on online content by targeting a platform’s design and business decisions. Conversely, if courts allow plaintiffs to characterize decisions about recommending, ranking, or presenting speech as mere “design,” then the same theory could become an increasingly broad way to bypass First Amendment protections for online expression— including for generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). For years, internet liability disputes largely revolved around content: who created a harmful post, who displayed it, and whether a platform could be treated as the publisher of someone else’s speech. Section 230 both prevents an interactive computer service from being liable for third-party content and grants them a safe harbor for content moderation decisions. Rather than blaming one post or video for causing harm or distress, the plaintiffs in K.G.M. argued that the platforms created an unsafe environment for their users by design. They claimed that the system was designed to encourage prolonged and compulsive use due to features like infinite scrolling without natural stopping points, autoplay without a new user decision, and recommendation systems continuously selecting material intended to hold the user’s attention. In a November 2025 pretrial ruling, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Carolyn Kuhl decided to allow a jury to conclude whether certain design features could cause harm independent of the specific content viewed. The court explained that companies may still face liability for harms arising from the design of their platforms simply because those design features also affect how information is communicated. In other words, the fact that a challenged feature has a communicative function does not necessarily shield the platform from liability for harms allegedly caused by the feature’s design. The jury ultimately agreed, finding that the platforms failed to exercise reasonable care in designing features that a reasonable person could foresee might be harmful to young users. K.G.M. echoes Lemmon v. Snap, Inc., a Ninth Circuit case that allowed a product liability claim to proceed against Snapchat. In that case, the plaintiffs alleged that Snapchat’s Speed Filter, which overlaid a user’s travel speed on any photo or video—combined with a reward system that encouraged users to share high-speed content—foreseeably encouraged dangerous driving and crashes. The Ninth Circuit specifically concluded that the duty to design a reasonably safe product was independent of Snap’s role in monitoring or publishing third-party content. Lemmon provides an important limiting principle for cases like K.G.M. A platform should not escape ordinary negligence law simply because a dangerous feature happens to exist within a communications service. But courts should require plaintiffs to identify an independently harmful design decision rather than allowing “design” more broadly to become another vehicle for challenging the dissemination of lawful speech. The problem arises when the alleged defect cannot be separated from the information being communicated. Recommendation systems and ranking mechanisms do not merely affect how long users remain on a service; they also determine which information reaches an audience. If liability arises whenever a recommendation system exposes someone to harmful or objectionable material, companies have an incentive to recommend less content, remove more borderline material, and limit access to controversial but lawful speech. While K.G.M. did not declare Instagram and YouTube defective products in every circumstance, the verdict reflects the court’s belief that companies can be liable for failing to use reasonable care during design. Courts should keep that theory narrow—claiming a platform is “addictive” should not be enough to win a trial. To meet the legal standard for negligent product design, plaintiffs should have to prove that: 1) any reasonable person could foresee that the design could be harmful to users; and 2) that the flawed design directly caused harm. Plaintiffs should have to identify a specific design choice, a foreseeable risk, a reasonable precaution, and a causal connection between the alleged failure and the injury before making a claim. Causation should be a major limit. Mental health injuries, for instance, rarely have one source. The sheer fact that a troubling feature exists does not prove that it caused a particular injury. The same framework should apply to GenAI. Although developers cannot escape all responsibility for safety merely because their choices were implemented through code, most AI development should be considered editorial decision-making, which is covered by the First Amendment. The question is whether an alleged harm arose from a design decision that independently created a foreseeable risk or whether a plaintiff’s claim merely objects to what an AI system communicated. A developer marketing a chatbot as a companion or source of emotional support may have a harder time claiming it assumed no responsibility for foreseeable reliance; however, K.G.M. demonstrates the risk of expanding that theory too far. Almost everything an AI system does ultimately reflects some design decision—from its training, system instructions, and safety mechanisms to its memory, interface, and rules governing how it responds. If the fact that an output resulted from “design” is enough to avoid traditional protections for speech, the distinction between content and conduct could lose all meaning. The practical consequence would be pressure on AI developers to make models more restrictive. Faced with uncertain liability, companies may limit responses involving controversial subjects, reduce access to sensitive but lawful information, or disable useful features altogether. Courts must therefore make a meaningful distinction between a defective mechanism that independently creates a foreseeable risk and a claim that ultimately objects to AI-generated speech. Comparative fault will remain a strong defense against broader claims. Companies should not be expected to prevent every determined user from circumventing a model’s protections. If a user repeatedly and deliberately defeats meaningful safeguards, then that conduct should matter when courts assess responsibility. The relevant question is not whether safeguards can ever be bypassed, but whether the company took reasonable precautions against foreseeable risks and whether the alleged harm resulted from the failure of those precautions. There should always be edge cases in which a truly malevolent or grossly negligent platform might face liability. But courts should set the bar high to avoid turning “product design” litigation into de facto speech regulation. Although that tradeoff ultimately places more burden on individual users to regulate their own interactions with these platforms, it is a better alternative to judges dictating the shape of emerging technologies. Liability is similarly plausible when a claim challenges independently wrongful conduct, such as knowingly ineffective age protections, deceptive safety claims, or failure to activate promised crisis tools. However, claims deserve greater scrutiny when they would require courts to dictate what lawful information a platform may communicate, how it must rank competing ideas, or which viewpoints an AI system must favor. That distinction matters because Section 230 was designed to prevent platforms from being treated as the publisher or speaker of third-party information. If a plaintiff can avoid that protection simply by describing recommendations, ranking, or other publishing functions as “defective design,” then the exception risks swallowing the rule. The effects would extend beyond the companies defending these lawsuits. Large platforms may be able to absorb years of litigation, but smaller platforms and emerging AI developers have fewer resources to do so. Faced with uncertain liability, the rational response may be to remove more material, recommend less information, and place tighter restrictions on what users can access. Liability intended to address harmful design could therefore indirectly restrict lawful online speech. Hopefully, K.G.M. does not mark the end of Section 230 or let every digital service be sued as defective products. The case proves that the distinction between publishing content and designing the systems around it is no longer theoretical. The law can and should hold companies responsible when their independently negligent choices create foreseeable harm; however, courts should not allow every dispute over online speech to become a product liability issue. The challenge is preserving both principles at once: A company should not be able to hide negligent product design behind Section 230, and a plaintiff should not be able to evade Section 230 merely by calling a publishing decision a design defect. Without that boundary, “design defect” risks becoming a side door for regulating online speech. 1411 K Street N.W., Suite 900
