title: LATEST: Date set for Haakon VIII’s oath as King of Norway following King Harald’s death - HOLA
content: King Harald of Norway died this Friday at the age of 89. Over the last 24 hours, his health was extremely serious after he was admitted to the hospital on August 17th for a blood disorder. Early in the morning, the Royal House announced the sad news about a man who was deeply loved by his people. Reactions have poured in and the entire country is in mourning. King Haakon VIII will take a solemn oath before the Norwegian Parliament, known as the Storting, on Tuesday, September 1, following the death of his father, King Harald V. The ceremony will see the new sovereign pledge to govern Norway in accordance with its Constitution and laws, formally underscoring his responsibilities within the country’s constitutional monarchy. King Harald died Friday at the age of 89. His health had become extremely serious during his final 24 hours after he was admitted to the hospital on August 17 with a blood disorder. The Royal House announced that the beloved monarch passed away at 6:35 a.m., prompting an outpouring of tributes as Norway entered a period of mourning. The late King’s coffin will be transported from Oslo University Hospital to the Royal Palace on Friday evening, accompanied by members of the royal family. It will later lie in state in the Palace Chapel, allowing members of the public to pay their respects before the funeral. The captain of the national soccer team, Martin Ødegaard, has joined the country in its grief, expressing his deepest condolences on Instagram. “Thank you for everything you meant to Norway. A wonderful king and a wonderful man with whom we all felt a close bond. Rest in peace, dear King Harald,” wrote the Drammen-born player alongside a photo of the King. The official website of the Norwegian Royal House has updated its institutional platform, adding the official portrait of Mette-Marit as Queen. With this visual update, the institution is adapting its digital presence to reflect the start of the new dynastic era alongside King Haakon VIII, reinforcing the public image of the sovereigns at the head of the Crown. The president of the Norwegian Parliament has paid tribute to King Harald V, highlighting the mourning of an entire nation after 35 years of a reign devoted to service and closeness to the people. In his words, he recalled the King’s historic role as the first prince born on Norwegian soil in more than five centuries, praising a brave and modern monarch who opened the Royal House to the people and to the world. The speech underlined the sovereign’s deep humanity, humor and empathy, recalling both his personal struggle to marry Queen Sonja and his ability to console the country during tragedies such as the July 22, 2011 attacks. After extending his condolences to the royal family, the president expressed the Norwegian people’s gratitude to the late monarch and looked with confidence to the new king, Haakon VIII, to guide the nation’s future. He closed his emotional address by marking this pivotal transition with solemn words: “An era has come to an end. A new one begins. The king is dead. Long live the king!” “Prime Minister and ministers. It is my duty to inform the Council of State that my beloved father, His Majesty King Harald V, passed away today, August 28, 2026, at 06:35, and that, in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, I have assumed the government as King of Norway. I will take the name Haakon VIII and will continue with the same motto chosen by my father, my grandfather and my great-grandfather: ‘All for Norway,’ as recorded in the minutes of the Council of State.” The Royal House has officially marked the beginning of the new reign by releasing the first official portrait of Haakon VIII as King of Norway, a historic image that captures the handover of the Crown after the formal succession ceremonies. In the photo, the King poses in full dress military uniform with the nation’s highest decorations, the same outfit he wore to the cabinet meeting at the Royal Palace with members of the Government, projecting the solemnity required of the head of state. The publication of this portrait formally opens a new dynastic chapter in the country’s history, as citizens celebrate the continuity of the institution. While inside the Royal Palace the ministers file in one by one to sign the institutional document, outside a large crowd holds an overwhelming silence, broken only by the solemn cannon salutes that announce the change of monarch, as they wait for the new King Haakon to step out onto the balcony to offer his first greeting as sovereign. Inside the Royal Palace, Government ministers are signing the institutional document one by one, while outside a gathered crowd maintains a respectful silence, waiting for the new king, Haakon, to appear on the balcony to greet them for the first time as sovereign. In a decisive step for the country’s institutional transition, the Government of Norway received the new monarch this morning at an extraordinary cabinet meeting held at the Royal Palace. During this formal encounter, the cabinet was officially informed of the sovereign’s death, and both the new king’s constitutional name and the motto that will guide his reign were presented publicly. This parliamentary and executive act follows the strict protocol triggered by the Crown upon the death of a sovereign. Before this meeting, the death was communicated to the president of the Storting (the Norwegian Parliament), the prime minister and the chief justice of the Supreme Court, as a preliminary step to the extraordinary government conference held before going to the Palace. With this cabinet audience, the nation formally begins a new dynastic era, guaranteeing the continuity of the State. In a clear sign of historical continuity, the new sovereign has decided to keep the traditional motto “Alt for Norge” (All for Norway), a historic phrase that has guided the Norwegian monarchy without interruption since the time of his great-grandfather, King Haakon VII. Philippe and Mathilde of Belgium have also offered their condolences following the death of Harald V, sending a warm message in which they highlighted his warmth, sense of humor and humanity. They remembered him as a sovereign who was very close to his citizens and as the oldest sitting monarch in Europe. The Belgian royals stressed that Harald V was a familiar, protective and constant presence for several generations in Norway. In their statement, they emphasized that for decades he acted as a pillar of stability for his nation, always guided by deep loyalty, steadfastness and a strong sense of duty. In Norway there is always a head of state. Article 6 of the Constitution sets out who are the legitimate heirs to the throne. After Harald’s death, the passing of the monarch is notified to the president of Parliament, the prime minister and the chief justice of the Supreme Court, the Government convenes an extraordinary meeting, the new King is received in a special session and is formally informed both of the death and of the new King’s name and motto. Haakon VIII must take an oral oath in Parliament. This is the first time in Norway’s recent history that the second in line to the throne is an adult; therefore, Princess Ingrid will take an oath in writing before Parliament. In the Kingdom of Norway there is always a monarch. When a King dies, his heir automatically assumes the throne. At the moment his father died, Haakon became Haakon VIII. The Norwegian Government has declared a period of national mourning from this Friday until after King Harald’s funeral. There are no clearly defined rules regarding the exact length of a national mourning period. King Felipe and Queen Letizia of Spain have also joined other monarchies in offering their condolences, with the following message: “With our respect and admiration for his person, and with deep sadness, we express our condolences for the loss of His Majesty King Harald V, an example of responsibility, dignity, simplicity and tireless dedication in the service of Norway and its people, both before and during his 35 years on the throne. Our condolences, with fraternal affection, to the Norwegian Royal Family.” The police have deployed additional personnel for all the ceremonies and for King Harald’s burial. Necessary security measures have been put in place, which involve traffic restrictions, and some areas in central Oslo will be completely closed to vehicles. After Haakon of Norway spent the entire night at his father’s side in the hospital, the new King has left the hospital with his wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, in an official car. Charles III of the United Kingdom has sent a personal message through the British Royal Family’s social media accounts. “With the deepest sadness, my wife and I learned of the death of my beloved cousin, King Harald V of Norway. For thirty-five years, King Harald served his people with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility. As Norway mourns the loss of such a remarkable figure, my family joins me in remembering a much-loved relative and friend, whose kindness, compassion and profound sense of duty have resonated across the sea and through the decades. The United Kingdom and Norway share exceptionally close historical and family ties, and Britain was one of the first countries to recognize Norway’s independence and establish diplomatic relations in 1905. These special bonds were strengthened further during the terrible trials of the Second World War and helped bring our two countries even closer together. The Queen and I send our deepest and most sincere condolences to Queen Sonja and all her family, as Britain shares Norway’s sorrow at this time of such a heartbreaking loss.” As of today, churches across Norway are open to anyone who wishes to light a candle and share in the nation’s grief, in all the country’s cathedrals and churches, according to a statement from the Church of Norway. Several members of the Royal Family went to the National Hospital and, a few hours later, several cars were seen leaving the building. Church bells across the country will ring for an hour this Friday at 12:00 noon to mark the King’s passing. “This is a day of mourning for us as a people and as a nation. At the same time, we feel gratitude,” said Bishop Olav Fykse Tveit. This tolling was coordinated with the Government and the Royal House and had already taken place when King Olav died in 1991. “Dear Haakon, with great sorrow we received the news that your father, King Harald, has died. Our thoughts are with all of you these days, with you, with Mette-Marit and with the rest of your family. Your father has meant so much to me and to us. With his calm manner and his perceptive gaze, King Harald was able to bring us all together. He was a good human being, with a sparkle in his eyes and a big heart. For 35 years, King Harald has been a solid point of unity for the Norwegian people. He joined duty and responsibility with closeness and humanity. He has been a role model for us and for many others. The ties between Denmark and Norway are strong. Over generations our families and our countries have been closely linked. Your father was an important part of all this, and it is with great sorrow that we feel his absence today. Now you are taking on your new role as King. It is a responsibility that we are convinced you will carry out with the same calm and dignity as your father. May peace, hope and affection be with you and give you strength on your path. Frederik and Mary.” The flags at Amalienborg are flying at half-mast. The Grand Duke and Grand Duchess of Luxembourg have sent the following message of comfort and support to the Norwegian Royal Family. “The death of His Majesty King Harald V plunges the Grand Duchess and me into deep sorrow. The weight of the years and the responsibilities assumed during his 35-year reign did not seem to affect his exceptional strength, will and endurance, which accompanied him throughout his life. World sailing champion (1987), then European champion (2005), having taken part in three Olympic Games (Tokyo 1964, Mexico City 1968 and Munich 1972), he was still competing in an international regatta in 2002, at the age of 85. Until his last day, he remained faithful to his motto: ‘All for Norway.’ In these delicate times for international relations, he wished to continue placing his broad experience in multilateral relations at the service of peace and the international community, in particular through his work on the awarding of the Nobel Peace Prize. The people of Luxembourg, the Grand Duchess and I, together with Grand Duke Henri and Grand Duchess Maria Teresa, offer his family and all Norwegians our most sincere condolences,” wrote Grand Duke Guillaume. “We are deeply saddened by the passing of His Majesty King Harald V of Norway. We cherish the memory of our special friendship with him. King Harald served his country with love, pride and conviction. Our trips together around Oslo and farther north are unforgettable. We are grateful for the way he welcomed the Netherlands and the Dutch people. In this time of sorrow, we extend our condolences to Queen Sonja, the Norwegian Royal Family and all Norwegians. King Harald remains in our thoughts as the personification of connection and friendship. Takk for alt (Thank you for everything),” read the statement, which was also endorsed by Princess Beatrix. “His work was characterized by his closeness to the people, and in our grief we also feel gratitude and deep respect for the unifying way in which he carried out his duties as king. Our deepest condolences to the family,” said the president of Parliament, Masud Gharahkhani. Following the death of King Harald, Carl Gustaf of Sweden has declared a period of mourning this Friday, which includes the cancellation of certain official activities planned for the Royal Family. The flags on all palaces and Crown buildings will fly at half-mast this Friday and Saturday. King Carl Gustaf was among the first to send his condolences to the Norwegian Royal Family, to whom he is bound by ties of blood and deep friendship. “With great sadness I have received the news of the death of our dear friend, King Harald. King Harald’s life story is exceptional. After enduring the hardships of war and exile in his childhood, he was able to return with his family to a free Norway and witness the remarkable development of the nation throughout the 20th century, before succeeding his father as King of Norway. Both as head of state and as a successful athlete, he was an outstanding representative of his country. He gave everything for Norway. Over the years, King Harald has been a good friend to me, my family and Sweden. Many in our country mourn the death of King Harald. Today, my family and I extend our deepest condolences to Queen Sonja. I wish my dear godson Haakon, who now succeeds his father as head of state, success and good fortune in the important role that awaits him in the service of our sister nation and its people.” “King Harald loved Norway and Norway loved its King,” said the country’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre. The Government will now meet to hold a press conference before gathering with the new King for an extraordinary cabinet meeting at the Palace. © ¡HOLA! title: Roger V. Lacerte Obituary - Lowell, MA (1935-2026) - Lowell Sun
content: Roger V. Lacerte died on August 25, 2026. He was 90. Roger was born in the Little Canada neighborhood of Lowell and immersed in the local Franco-American community. ‘La Francophonie’ became his lifelong passion. A self-described ‘cut-up’ in school, he became the first in his immediate family to complete high school and even went on to earn a PhD. He taught high school and collegiate French for five decades. Roger also published L’Unite, a Lewiston, ME, monthly newspaper; hosted several radio programs, notably Chez Nous (1998-2022); and ran the Manchester, NH, bookstore La Librairie Populaire (1962-2022). A founder and leader in fraternal organizations, such as the Club Richelieu de Lowell, and historical groups, such as the Societe historique franco-americaine, Roger was recognized as the Franco-American of the Year in Lowell and Manchester (2007 and 2010, respectively). Roger was known for his charisma and joie de vivre’ever a song in his heart, a twinkle in his eye, and a joke on his lips. He died Tuesday at his childhood home, surrounded by family and friends. Visitation will take place 9:30-11:30 am on August 28 at Laurin Funeral Home, Lowell; prayers and interment to follow at St Joseph Cemetery, Chelmsford. Copyright 2026 Lowell Sun. title: “Potpourri V” - Wilcox Newspapers
content: I am pleased to state that the local police persons are earning their keep these days. They had a vulture hit a vehicle and a vehicle hit a deer and, most of all, the BS-OT Police handled 59 calls the week of July 6. Those of my column readers will remember several years ago, during one of the reoccurring tax renewal votes, my questioning about why us honest taxpayers here in the Village and the surrounding Oronoko Township were being asked to pay a million dollars per year for this constabulary service when most of what we knew they were doing was by observing the police cars pulling over motorists and bothering them. I may have said something about the make and model of the vehicles involved in this police action and their reports as irrelevant information that gave no real information and merely bothered some of us. Anyhow, I now all the more appreciate the work of Melodie Wright in composing this report for the paper, feeling responsible for putting her through this added task.   You will notice that I have matured a bit and no longer complain about the million dollars a year. You can check the July 15 issue of this fine paper.  They handled “one incorrigible” and “four civil /family disputes.” I wonder what the incorrigible person was doing, but really do not want to know because I assume that they keep doing it over and over which, I can only also assume, irritates the police persons. The family disputes are the most dangerous as well as the least psychologically satisfying type of police work there is. It is in this work that most of the police get shot. I can also assume domestic police work is the most important as any time there is a homicide one or the other of the spouses is the prime suspect. The worst thing about these disputes is that minor children are often around—in fact they may be the only innocent people involved—and growing up is difficult enough without having to endure the stress of the yelling and screaming and hitting. I am slowly catching up here, and so, referring to the Looking Back in the August 5 issue under 113 years ago I notice that George T. Kimmel has resigned his position with the Kawneer Company of Niles. As I vaguely recall, Kawneer was in the steel door frame business for office and commercial buildings. They may have done other things, but I was not around then to find out.  At one time Niles was full of light industry—National Standard making tire bead wire at 300,000 psi tensile strength, which is similar to piano wire, Simplicity making tissue paper patterns for sewing clothes at home, Tyler for making commercial grocery store chest refrigerators and freezers, the French paper mill for making stationary, and we must not forget the mushroom factory on Third Street that turned composted horse manure into mushrooms. Most of these businesses did not last past the third generation as that is about when the fire went out of the belly, causing investment in new modern facilities to falter and tight management to end. There was even a large steam locomotive repair operation complete with a round house, that still exists but not functioning as anything to do with railroads. We now have some smaller dynamic industries, such as Niles Precision on Fort Street, currently owned and managed by one of my cousins.  My grandfather did not become George Kimmel Senior until 1917 when my father—Junior—was born and that tradition has continued until my poor grandson, such a bright and innocent little person that he is, is now labelled number V. I do not know for certain when my Grandparents were married, but my Aunt Mary Jane was born in 1912—the same year as Loris Sherburn and several other luminaries and she spent her life keeping her birthday and her parents’ wedding day widely separated making it more difficult for the local gossips to have something more to gossip about. I do know that my grandfather was very poor and thus when he and Martha Boone decided to get married he had to go to Detroit to work for a month to earn money for the wedding, and then when he took the train back to town he met several of his cousins at the local bar and they kept encouraging him to drink a little more so that he could make more political speeches, to everyone’s great entertainment, such that they kept passing the hat and asking for more speeches. When word finally came back to Martha, who was living then at the Shaker Farm with her parents, she rapidly went to the barn and hooked up the horse to the buggy and drove into town to unceremoniously drag my grandfather out of the bar. By then it was a little too late as the money had been spent and so he had to go back to Detroit for another month before they could marry. He could get a job anywhere as he was a good talker and a pleasant person and always had a good job all through the Depression and that facility along with desperation explains him working for Kawneer for a while and then leaving them. My research assistant found out why he was so poor by finding part of a handwritten history of the Kimmel family written by Suzie Mars, who was my grandfather’s cousin, ten years older. If anyone has the other part, the first ten pages of this essay, we would really appreciate it.  The one thing that really stands out about life in pioneer times is the amount of death in this time before vaccines and antibiotics and good medical care.  Mothers died in childbirth, children died of infectious diseases, adults died of tuberculosis and my great-great-grandfather Samuel Kimmel (1803-1854) died of typhoid fever when my great-grandfather was twelve years old. Samuel’s second wife had used the opportunity to clean the house out of the family silver and moved to the middle of Illinois where she had family. The Kimmel family was so destitute that the children were farmed out to various local families and my great-grandfather George Henry Kimmel (1842-1913) went to the Stemm family and that is doubtless how he met his first wife, Ally Stemm, who died of an infectious disease while assisting a neighboring family with care of their children was also stricken with the disease. She is buried over in Union Cemetery just south of Hinchman. And now a brief return to current events in our town. You can tell that it is a slow news week when the most exciting thing going on was the paving of Main Street by applying a single seal. I had planned on a long disquisition on the subject of single seals and double seals until I figured out that I did not know enough. In reality, the writer does not have to know much about the subject at hand, but they had better be certain that they know more than any of the readers of his column. I cannot handle more letters to the editor, being a sensitive artistic type, and so I am starting to equivocate more. I was quite excited about this street paving excitement until they put an extra layer of tar on top of the crushed rock of the single seal which confused me because it was not really tar, but something that dried quickly and so was not sticky like tar while binding the rock chunks together. I had never seen that done before and thus am unable to go on and on. All I know for certain is that this method of paving is cheaper than laying down concrete or asphalt and it is a lot better than mud puddles, pot holes, and dust. And then I got all excited again about a local news opportunity when I saw some tall wild grass-looking plants in the ditch alongside Shawnee Road just about half way between the Township Hall and the Fire Person’s and Police Person’s Public Safety building. At first I thought that it was Phragmites australis, which is the tall grass that one sees all along the freeways and tollways going through Gary, Indiana that is terribly invasive completely covering any swamp crowding out all native plants so I did a short drive on I-80 as that is how this plant gets spread all across the U.S. of A., growing in the ditches of the limited access roads and noticed a different color seed plume from our local plant, which means it is probably Arondo donax, a tall grass that has the same leaf pattern as does corn. And thus I do not get to go on and on about invasive plants from other countries. The more I think about it the less certain I am of its identity.  When I get the time I will drive down Lauer Road to look at a known stand of Phragmites australis. A report will follow. There is an interesting and topical story about Nancy Pelosi and Arondo donax which grows very thick along the Rio Grande on this side of the border and gets about twelve feet tall. Back when illegal mass migration was taking place along our southern border, aided by NGOs who were making good money from our government payments for their skills at the facilitation of these caravans and I will spare you the memory of that upsetting time by naming the President then. They had made trails through this grass enough to squeeze through well hidden from above and everywhere else. When this was brought to Pelosi’s attention, her comment was for them to mow the grass, accompanied by arm motions of pushing a lawn mower. I guess the word ‘grass’ has several connotations which is why us professional horticulturists use the Linnean Binomial Nomenclature, and not just to show off to the hoi polloi. Further amusement was provided by an Associated Press release printed in the July 22 Herald-Palladium entitled “2 more convictions thrown out in 2020 plot to kidnap Michigan governor”. As you will recall, at the time I looked at the mug shots of the people arrested for this offence and stated that none of them looked smart enough to be a threat to anyone for anything. I believe that it was reported that the police had a real police person acting as an undercover agent present at all of the training sessions and meetings of this illustrious group and he was finally instructed to get them organized and on the stick to get along with the kidnapping plans as the police were tired of waiting. If it were me I would have requested a brighter looking group to infiltrate so that I would not have had to do all of the hard organization and implementation work. It appeared that the defense would have been Entrapment, but that was not the case. The core elements of Entrapment appear to have happened in this case—Government Inducement and Lack of Predisposition. There are two legal tests used by the courts—the Federal and some states use the Subjective Test of focusing on the defendant’s mind—to see if he (they) were predisposed to commit the crime. California and a few other states use the Objective Test which focuses on police conduct, meaning that the police would push a normal, law-abiding person to commit a crime.  Anyhow, the newspaper report is that three people had their convictions thrown out on technical grounds. “The appeals court said kidnapping is not an underlying violent felony that can support a conviction under Michigan’s terrorism law.” One of the three people had moved out of state weeks before the FBI made arrests and the other two said that they were no longer in contact with the key figures in this plot at the time the FBI made their move. To finish up this article: “Whitmer, a Democrat, was never physically harmed. Undercover FBI agents and informants were inside Fox’s group for months, and the scheme was broken up.” The news media, at the time, assumed that this was a real authentic plot by real violent revolutionaries and overlooked the fact that the criminal justice system had charged them under the wrong law. In my ongoing quest to bring accurate, topical, and important information to the readership of this find newspaper, here is my latest attempt—this time it is an explanation of why our local health clinic, the one located just beside the late Apple Valley parking lot and that used to be called “University Medical Clinic” has been referred to by the Corwell hospital computer as the Watervliet Hospital Medical Clinic. When I first saw this the computer did not even know how to spell ‘Watervliet’, and that is because: “Watervliet means flowing water in Dutch, coming from water and vliet which is a Dutch word for a minor streaming water, though it may refer to a city canal or a river that connects such flows.” This saga began back in 1977. Artificial Intelligence says that: “A Federal Rural Health Clinic (RHC) is a certified outpatient facility established by the 1977 Rural Health Clinic Services Act to provide primary care and basic lab services in underserved rural areas, backed by special Medicare and Medicaid cost-based reimbursements.”  The requirements are that it must be in a non-urban area designated as a health shortage or underserved area, and has a team approach to staffing using physicians alongside nurse practitioners, physician assistants, or certified nurse-midwives with mid-level providers staffing the clinic and the focus is on primarily outpatient primary care and routine diagnostic lab work and then it qualifies for ‘special federal payment structures to help clinics stay open in remote regions’. And we can thus conclude that either Corwell is extra sharp with the kinds of office workers who spend their time figuring out how to scam the Medicare and Medicaid systems out of more money or that the original people who set up, started, and funded this facility had a conscience or maybe a sense of ethics. I am hesitant to go any further down this road as I am the beneficiary of the scam, having used this clinic for years and having the people there dedicated to saving my life and prolonging it. As you can see, the only medical facility in this area that qualifies as being ‘rural’ is the one up in Watervliet, and so for billing and legal purposes this local clinic had a name change. I can understand how many of you were confused and probably thought there was some clerical error at Corewell up in St. Joe.  Glad I could help with the confusion and hope that you have not lost faith in the government takeover of the health care in our country, at least formerly the Land of the Free. Humor is further provided by the government take over being labelled: “The Affordable Health Care Act” at the time it was enacted.  The mainstream news media did not predict how this all was doomed to fail in every aspect that it claimed to improve things. Because we live in one of the most prolific fruit, berry (brambles), and vegetable producing areas of the world, I like to comment on what it is like to be a farmer. I notice that farmers tend to spend their time battling nature, squabbling with governmental regulations of everything from agricultural chemical controls to migrant labor specific rules and the new regulations about heat exposure. And this summer we have rain and heat and drought to deal with.  One of my key employees used to work for the late George Stover and thus knows of what he speaks.  Serbando recently told me that when it rains the farmers have to spray every other day. Rain washes the spray dope off the fruit and leaves. The spray costs $1,200 per tankful. I did not get the details on what the spray was for. However, as I recall, peaches get brown rot when it rains, and maybe split pits, and then apples get scab. I have been out of that business for some time and am not up on the details.  When it rains strawberries get sun scald and the rain splashes sand onto the strawberries. As I started to say, farmers are too busy working to write about their business and so us scriveners get to say whatever we remember or can make up. The truth is out there someplace. Besides everything else we can worry about politics and ideology and the apocalypse. For this subject I consulted the August 8-9 WSJ OPINION section and specifically Peggy Noonan’s ever topical op-ed, this time entitled: Socialism Is Here—and It’s Serious.  Peggy Noonan is my wife’s favorite writer.  She read one of Peggy’s earlier books where she talks about her time being Reagan’s speech writer, and was impressed. I am rushed for time these days and will only be able to string a few sentences together from this op-ed piece. You will get the general thrust of the essay. The first sentence is: “Socialism is not a passing thing, but an arriving thing. It must be taken seriously …” And in comparison to the early twentieth century Wobblies (IWW people) she says:  “Today’s socialists strike me as colder, less human, fiercer and occasionally sociopathic. In general, they appear to have an idea of history rather than attachments to existing people and institutions.  Most strike me not as people who love America and wish to make it better, but people ready to exploit its freedoms to build a movement that, if successful would transform America’s fundamental nature. It will no longer be the freedom place …” “As religion recedes, politics takes its place.  The young have been educated within a general framework of assumptions and language of the left—structures of power, oppressor groups, critical theory, intersectionality.”  The alert here will remember that I have made a few feeble attempts at explaining intersectionality, and it is difficult to do if one does not understand anything at all about it in the first place. At least I understood that it was important and dangerous. “It’s our view here that free-market capitalism is organic and flows upward from the human person—man wants to build, trade, invent, provide for and rise, and he erects laws and a way of economic being that allows the realizations of those desires. Economic freedom works with human nature.” “Socialism is a more abstract and ideological vision of justice that doesn’t flow up but must be imposed from the top down. It isn’t based on the natural, or on man as he is; it’s a construct that involves coercion.” “Socialism is a belief, and it summons feeling. Capitalism is a thing of reason, a disadvantage in an age of sensation.” If you want a longer, and ipso facto more in-depth study I recommend a book I have mentioned before: The Passing of an Illusion, The Idea of Communism in the Twentieth Century by Francois Furet, all 596 pages. Here from p. 166: “Lenin and Mussolini emerged from the same political family—that of revolutionary socialism.”  And so that is what we have to look forward to if this trend continues. Try to not think about it, or you will all be jumping off the bridge instead of using it to come into town.  Mussolini invented fascism that influenced the Nazis and we know how that turned out. Lenin set up the basic structure of Russia and we know how that turned out, with millions dying of starvation or while slaving in the Gulag. As long as we are ending on a down note, I have to confess to being asleep at the switch and missed the opportunity, a month or so ago, of reminding everyone of one of the great local events, a violin concert by Carla Trynchuk, who artificial intelligence states is “an accomplished concert violinist”. She is really good, a natural, who has devoted her life to learning and practicing that art. I am sorry for not keeping up on that scheduled concert.

title: King Harald V of Norway obituary - The Guardian
content: Monarch who opened up the Norwegian royal family and its palaces to the public, and married a commoner despite his father’s opposition King Harald V of Norway, who has died aged 89, Europe’s oldest serving monarch, was the country’s third king since it regained independence in 1905 following the dissolution of its union with Sweden. Although he ceased to be head of the Lutheran state church in 2012 and subsequently lost his constitutional status as “holy” six years later, he did exhibit the Scandinavian moderation, stoicism and genial approachability that led a newspaper to name him Norway’s person of the year in 2017. The first Norwegian king to be born in the country since 1370, Harald was also related to both the Swedish and the British royal families. His parents were Crown Prince Olav, who was king as Olav V between 1957 and 1991, and his wife, Princess Märtha, a member of the Swedish royal dynasty. His grandparents were King Haakon VII, the first king of the independent country, who reigned for 52 years from 1905, and his wife, Queen Maud, daughter of Britain’s Edward VII. The family roots are Danish – from the Glücksburg dynasty – as were those of the Duke of Edinburgh and the former Greek royal family. The mixed heritage made him sympathetic to refugees: “It is not easy to say where we come from. Home is where the heart is,” he said. He was Queen Elizabeth II’s second cousin and a knight of the garter. At the time of his birth, Harald was 16th in line to the British throne, though he had fallen in the rankings to around 80th in more recent years. Confusingly, he was not the fifth Harald to rule his country, but the sixth – the 10th-century Harald Bluetooth generally not being assigned a number in the list of Norwegian kings. The king never attracted a picturesque title as did some of his Viking predecessors – such as Bluetooth, Harald Fairhair and Harald Hardrada, who tried to seize the English throne a few weeks before the Norman invasion in 1066 and was killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge. Harald himself was only three at the time of the Nazi invasion of Norway in 1940, and he and his mother and two older sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, initially fled to Sweden, which, trying to maintain its neutrality while accommodating the Germans’ attack on their neighbour, was reluctant to let them in. It is alleged that the royal party was initially turned back at the border, and allowed to proceed only when the driver of their car threatened to ram it through the border post. Within three months, Harald, his sisters and mother had escaped to the US. They spent the war years in Washington DC and Harald thereafter spoke English with a slight American accent. Meanwhile, Harald’s grandfather and father escaped to England, where they led a government in exile. Famously Haakon, turning up at the BBC to make a broadcast to his people, was asked by a receptionist: “Where did you say you were king of, dear?” Following the liberation of Norway at the end of the war, the family was reunited and Harald was enrolled first at a state primary and then at Oslo cathedral school. From there he studied at Oslo University and the Norwegian military academy, before following in his father’s footsteps to read history, economics and politics at Balliol College, Oxford, where he also rowed for the college. A keen competitive yachtsman, he and his crews represented Norway at successive Olympics in Tokyo in 1964, Mexico City in 1968 and Munich in 1972, and won world championship medals through the 1980s and a European championship gold medal in 2005. If this was a conventional career, much less so was his determination to marry a commoner, Sonja Haraldsen, a shop assistant who was the daughter of an Oslo textile manufacturer, whom he had met at a sailing party in 1959. The friendship was kept secret for several years, partly because of Olav’s reluctance to have the heir to the throne marry someone who was not royal. In the end, Harald forced the issue by declaring to his father that if he was not allowed to marry her he would not marry anyone, thus bringing an end to the dynasty. The couple married in 1968. Harald was sworn in as king automatically following Olav’s death in January 1991. Although lacking his father’s easy bonhomie, the king attempted successfully – and popularly – to open up the institution and its palace and estates more freely to the public. The Norwegian monarch’s duties are similar to those in Britain, with non-exercised executive power, and all official acts having to be endorsed by the governing council of state, equivalent to a British cabinet. The Norwegian parliament constitutionally debates whether to continue the monarchy every four years, and earlier this year, despite controversies concerning the royal family, voted in favour of its continuation by 141 to 26. The greatest crisis in the country’s modern history occurred on 22 July 2011 when the domestic terrorist Anders Behring Breivik murdered 77 people, mainly at a young socialists’ holiday camp on Utøya island. The king attracted public praise in the wake of the tragedy, when he met bereaved relatives and called for national solidarity and mutual support. He was seen to weep at the memorial service for the victims. Harald was treated for bladder cancer in 2003, contracted Covid, had a pacemaker fitted in 2024 and was being treated for the blood disorder haemolytic anaemia. He is survived by Sonja and their children, Princess Märtha Louise and Prince Haakon, whose wife, Mette-Marit (nee Tjessem-Høiby), was obliged to apologise in February this year for email exchanges with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in which her name was mentioned nearly 1,000 times. The king said that she had not broken any law. Mette-Marit’s son by a previous relationship, Marius, was jailed for four years in June following convictions for two rapes and drug offences. Haakon succeeds Harald as King Haakon VIII and will adopt the monarchy’s traditional motto: “All for Norway”. Harald V, king of Norway, born 21 February 1937; died 28 August 2026

This information will not be used or disclosed for any purpose other than for processing this request. King Harald V of Norway has died at 89 from complications related to hemolytic anemia. The latest update from the royal house early Thursday morning reported that the king’s condition was very serious and that his entire family, including his grandchildren, had rushed to the hospital in Oslo where he was receiving treatment. According to Norwegian media reports, Marius Borg Høiby was also at his bedside. Crown Prince Haakon and Crown Princess Mette-Marit were dressed in black, with the crown prince wearing a black tie. Immediately after the news broke, people began gathering in the square in front of the royal palace in Oslo, bringing flowers and rallying in memory of their king. This content can also be viewed on the site it originates from. The monarch was deeply loved by his people. His reign reflected the Norwegian royal motto “Alt for Norge,” or “Everything for Norway.” Born in 1937, his life was marked by war, exile, his love for the commoner Sonja, his long apprenticeship as crown prince, and, finally, more than three decades on the throne. In his New Year’s address delivered on the evening of December 31, 2022, King Harald spoke to the many challenges facing Norway, Europe, and the world—the climate crisis, the war in Ukraine following the Russian invasion, and the rising number of refugees immigrating to the continent. In that speech, the monarch, then 84 years old, urged Norwegians not to let fear overwhelm them. According to Harald, it is precisely in times of greatest difficulty that some of the most valuable qualities of Norwegian society emerge: empathy, humanity, and a sense of community. Values that, in his view, have always served as a bulwark against crises and divisions. These words also aptly describe how the king interpreted his role as monarch. His life story was one of transformation. It was the story of a child forced to leave his home because of the war, of a young prince who had to wait nine years before he could marry the woman he loved, and of a king who made closeness to ordinary people one of the pillars of the monarchy. Throughout his long reign, Harald sought to remain close to his citizens, listen to them, and represent a modern, open, and inclusive Norway. Norwegians considered him not only their king, but a deeply familiar figure, holding a cultural significance akin to the late Queen Elizabeth II in the United Kingdom. Harald V was born on February 21, 1937, in Skaugum, Asker, the residence of the crown prince’s family. He was the son of Crown Prince Olav—who would become King Olav V—and Crown Princess Märtha. His grandfather was King Haakon VII. The first prince of Norwegian descent born in 567 years, his birth held special significance for the young Norwegian monarchy. Before him, Olav and Märtha had had two daughters, princesses Ragnhild and Astrid, but at the time, the law of succession excluded women from the throne. With Harald’s birth, the male line of succession to the crown was secured. In 1990, the Norwegian Constitution was amended to introduce primogeniture without distinction of sex for those born after the amendment took effect. Due to this legislative timing, Crown Prince Haakon, born in 1973, will inherit the throne from Harald ahead of his older sister, Märtha Louise, while Haakon’s daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, born in 2004, is ahead of her brother Sverre Magnus. King Harald belonged to one of Europe’s great dynastic families. Through his paternal grandmother, Queen Maud—daughter of England’s King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra—Harald was, in fact, a great-grandson of Queen Victoria. This made him a relative of numerous European monarchs at the time. A photo of King Harald as a child with his parents, King Olav V and Princess Märtha of Sweden, and his two sisters He spent the first three years of his life peacefully in Skaugum, together with his sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid. But on April 9, 1940, when Nazi Germany invaded Norway, everything changed. The royal family was forced to flee. Little Harald, just three years old, left with his mother and sisters while King Haakon VII and Crown Prince Olav were active in the Norwegian resistance. After passing through Sweden, Märtha and her three children settled in the United States. The crown princess had managed to take the children far from occupied Europe in part to prevent Harald from becoming a tool of Nazi propaganda. At the time, there was a fear that the Germans might attempt to depose Haakon VII and turn the young prince into a puppet king. For nearly five years, Harald lived far from his homeland at a Pooks Hill residence near Washington, DC. The family was welcomed with special attention by US president Franklin D. Roosevelt. Safe on the other side of the Atlantic, he also had the opportunity to get to know firsthand the Norwegian military personnel serving in the war. When he visited the Norwegian Air Force training center near Toronto, the prince became something of a mascot for the Norwegian pilots. When Germany surrendered in May 1945, Harald was finally able to return home. On June 7, 1945, together with his mother and sisters, he arrived in Oslo, where a huge crowd welcomed the royal family’s return. He was eight years old. After returning to Norway, Harald began attending Smestad Skole in Oslo, a public school. The choice had symbolic significance: The future king was to grow up understanding the everyday reality of his peers. In 1956, he joined the armed forces and attended the Cavalry Officers’ School, later continuing his studies at the Krigsskolen. Military training would remain an important part of his life. Over the years, he would rise to the ranks of general in the army and air force and admiral in the navy. In 1960, he left for the United Kingdom. He studied political science, history, and economics at Balliol College, Oxford—the same college that his father had attended. Harald also had to cope with another great family loss. His mother, Princess Märtha of Sweden, died of cancer in 1954, at the age of just 53. Harald was only 17 years old. When his father, Olav V, became king in 1957, Harald became crown prince. From that moment on, he began to carry out an increasing number of official duties alongside his father. In 1958, he served as regent for the first time during the king’s absence. Harald also began traveling abroad to represent Norway and to promote the country’s economic interests. He took part in numerous missions with trade delegations, helping to open doors for Norwegian businesses. This was an activity he would continue even after his accession to the throne. The then Prince Harald with his fiancée Sonja Haraldsen As a young man, Harald had to fight to marry the woman he loved. He had met Sonja Haraldsen, a young middle-class woman from Oslo, the daughter of fabric merchants, and a bond had formed between them that was destined to last a lifetime. For an heir to the throne, however, marrying a woman without royal blood or a noble title was discouraged. Their love became a matter of state, and the couple had to wait nine years for an answer. There were fears that a commoner could damage the monarchy, with some suggesting that such a marriage could spell an end for the monarch. Finally, after consulting with parliamentary leaders and the government, King Olav gave his consent. On March 19, 1968, it was officially announced that Crown Prince Harald would marry Sonja. The wedding took place on August 29, 1968, at Oslo Cathedral. After nine years of waiting, Harald had finally married the woman he loved. (Possibly at the displeasure of Queen Frederica of Greece, who was rumored to have set her sights set on Harald as a husband for her daughter, Sofia, the future Queen of Spain.) August 29 would have marked their 58th wedding anniversary. The wedding day of the then Prince Harald and Sonja Haraldsen After the wedding, Harald and Sonja moved to Skaugum, the residence traditionally associated with the crown prince and princess. On September 22, 1971, their first daughter, Princess Märtha Louise, was born. On July 20, 1973, Prince Haakon was born. For many years, Harald and Sonja raised their family away from the spotlight, preparing for the roles that awaited them. As time went on, grandchildren were born. In 2001, Harald and Sonja became grandparents when Haakon married Mette-Marit, who joined the royal family along with her son, Marius Borg Høiby. Märtha Louise and Ari Behn had three daughters: Maud Angelica, Leah Isadora, and Emma Tallulah. In 2004, Princess Ingrid Alexandra was born—she was second in line to the throne after her father—and in 2005, Prince Sverre Magnus was born. When King Olav V fell ill in the spring of 1990, Harald assumed the duties of regent. Then, on January 17, 1991, King Olav died, and Harald became King of Norway. The new monarch took the oath of allegiance to the Constitution before the Storting. On June 23, 1991, he was crowned at Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim. He chose to retain his family’s motto, “Alt for Norge.” The transition from crown prince to monarch was not easy. Like Elizabeth II in the UK, Harald had to develop his own style and strike a delicate balance between tradition and modernity. King Harald V of Norway (right), seated next to Queen Sonja, takes the oath as the new monarch of Norway before the Storting (the Norwegian Parliament) in Oslo on January 21, 1991 Outside of his official duties, Harald has always had two great passions: nature and sports. He loved hunting and fishing and was an avid salmon angler. In the fall, he took part in moose hunts in the Sikkilsdalen area. Environmental protection was another of his major interests. As crown prince he was one of the founders of the Norwegian chapter of the Worldwide Fund for Nature and served as its president for 20 years. In 2013, he also fulfilled a personal dream by visiting the Indigenous peoples of the Amazon. But it was sailing where Harald made his greatest mark as an athlete. He competed in three Olympic Games: Tokyo 1964, Mexico City 1968, and Munich 1972. In Tokyo, he placed eighth in the 5.5-meter class and also served as Norway’s flag bearer during the opening ceremony. Over the years, he achieved significant international successes in sailing. In 1987, aboard the Fram X, he became world champion in the one-ton class. In 2005, by then a veteran of the sport, he won the offshore-sailing European Championship with the Fram XV. His sporting career earned him numerous awards, including the prestigious Holmenkollen Medal in 2007. In 2025, he also received the highest honor from the Norwegian Sports Federation (Norges Idrettsforbund), becoming an honorary member. Harald continued to compete in national and international regattas until 2022, when he announced the end of his competitive career. For decades, the monarch also followed ski competitions and numerous other sporting events, so much so that he jokingly referred to himself as a “sports idiot,” a true sports fanatic. King Harald sailing with the then Prince Felipe of Spain, who was also passionate about sailing His relationship with the Norwegian people was one of the most important aspects of his reign. Harald sought to be a monarch close to his citizens and to represent a modern, open, and inclusive Norway. One of the royal couple’s most symbolically significant projects was their journey through Norway’s municipalities. Visiting people in their communities and gaining firsthand insight into Norway’s diverse realities became a fundamental part of their work. With planned visits to Siljan and Nissedal in Telemark, as well as communities in Trøndelag, he and Queen Sonja had nearly reached their goal of visiting every municipality in Norway. King Harald of Norway with Queen Sonja and the crown prince and princess One of the most defining aspects of Harald’s reign was his focus on inclusion and diversity. A particularly significant moment came in 2016, when, during a celebration marking the 25th anniversary of his accession to the throne, the king delivered one of his most famous speeches. Speaking about Norwegian society, Harald emphasized that the country belongs to everyone: “Norwegians are young and old, high and low, able-bodied and wheelchair users…. Norwegians are rich, poor, and in between…. Norwegians are unmarried, divorced, families, and old couples. Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who like boys, and girls and boys who are fond of each other…. Norwegians believe in God, Allah, everything and nothing.” Another speech that has remained in the collective memory was the one delivered in Kiberg in 1992, during a trip to northern Norway. Harald paid tribute to the Norwegian partisans who had fought alongside the Soviets during World War II, helping to restore the memory of a segment of the population that had long been marginalized in the official narrative of the war. Among the most dramatic moments of Harald’s reign were the terrorist attacks of July 22, 2011, which included a car bomb explosion in Oslo and a mass shooting at a summer camp. At a memorial service at Oslo Cathedral, the king did not hide his tears. In his speech, delivered during the national commemoration at Oslo Spektrum, he emphasized the importance of solidarity, freedom, and coexistence in a multicultural society. In recent years, the king’s health has become an increasingly important part of his story. In 2003, he was diagnosed with bladder cancer. He underwent surgery at the Radiumhospitalet in Oslo and resumed his official duties in the spring of 2004. After the surgery, he also quit smoking. In 2005, the king had to undergo another surgery, this time on his heart, for subvalvular aortic stenosis. He had an artificial heart valve implanted at Rikshospitalet hospital. In the years that followed, there were other episodes that required hospital treatment or periods of convalescence. In 2017, he was hospitalized for an infection; in 2019 and 2020, he was temporarily placed on sick leave due, respectively, to a viral infection and health issues that required further investigation. In January 2021, he underwent surgery for a tendon injury above his right knee. In March 2022, he tested positive for COVID-19, fortunately with only mild symptoms. In August of that same year, he was hospitalized for an infection that required intravenous antibiotic treatment. Another hospitalization was necessary in December 2022, again due to an infection. In February 2024, Harald contracted an infection while on a private vacation in Langkawi, Malaysia. The infection caused an irregular heart rhythm, and doctors decided to temporarily implant a pacemaker. The king was subsequently transferred to Norway on a medical flight. At Rikshospitalet in Oslo, he received a permanent pacemaker. After a total of more than two weeks in the hospital, between Malaysia and Norway, Harald was discharged and began his recovery. In February 2026, the king was hospitalized again while on a private vacation abroad, this time in Tenerife. He was treated for an infection and dehydration. Despite everything, Harald never considered abdicating the throne. This decision deeply reflects the monarch’s long-held view of his role. Harald has repeatedly stated that he considers the monarchy a lifelong commitment. Despite his age and health issues, he has therefore always publicly ruled out abdication, saying that his oath is for life. The king’s difficulty walking as he leaned on two crutches In addition to King Harald’s health problems and those of Queen Sonja, who has been struggling with heart conditions, the Norwegian monarchy has also had to face a series of scandals in recent years involving the younger generations. Crown Princess Mette-Marit, wife of Crown Prince Haakon, has been at the center of controversy over her past ties to Jeffrey Epstein. Mette-Marit herself has publicly acknowledged that she made a mistake by not vetting Epstein’s background more carefully. In addition, Mette-Marit underwent a lung transplant in June of this year, following years of health issues related to chronic pulmonary fibrosis diagnosed in 2018. Before the surgery, her condition had progressively worsened, to the point where she occasionally needed oxygen. Even more serious was the case of Marius Borg Høiby, Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship. His involvement in criminal proceedings and the allegations of rape and assault against him, resulting in a conviction on two counts of rape and a four-year prison sentence, have cast a particularly difficult light on the crown prince’s family. The daughter of King Harald and Queen Sonja, Princess Märtha Louise, has also followed a path far removed from traditional royal life. The rebellious princess renounced her official duties, and she has attracted significant attention over the years for her personal and professional choices. Her first husband, from whom she later divorced, died by suicide. And her marriage to American shaman Durek Verrett, which took place in 2024, sparked fresh controversy over the relationship between the monarchy, celebrity, and private life. Harald and Sonja, however, have always chosen to support their daughter, even when her unconventional decisions caused controversy. Norway has lost one of its most popular and beloved monarchs, who, during his reign, won over his subjects with his level-headedness, warmth, and trustworthiness. Now Haakon will take the reins. In Norway, the succession to the throne is much faster than in the United Kingdom. The fundamental difference is that there is no longer a coronation, and the new monarch automatically becomes king upon the death of his predecessor. Article Nine of the Constitution stipulates that, upon ascending the throne, the monarch must take an oath before the Storting, the Norwegian parliament, to govern the country in accordance with the Constitution and the laws. In addition, the new king will receive a solemn ecclesiastical blessing in Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim. The crown jewels are placed on the high altar without being worn. In an official statement today, Norway prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre marked the passing of Harald and the transition to a new era. “It is comforting to know that King Haakon will reign under the same motto as his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather before him: We give our all for Norway,” he said. “An era has ended. A new era is beginning. The king is dead. Long live the king!” The Norwegian royal family with the crown prince and princess A photo of the royal family during an official event A Posh Visual History of Prince William and Prince Harry at Eton A Close-Up Look at Some of the Most Spectacular Royal Fashion Plates What Queen Elizabeth Really Thought of Harry and Meghan A Long, Glamorous History of British Royals at The Carlyle Hotel From the Archive: Princess Margaret’s Doomed Romance © 2026 Condé Nast. title: The Sweetest Photos from King Harald V’s Youth - Town & Country Magazine
content: King Harald V of Norway passed away this week at the age of 89. Here, we take a look back at the late monarch’s young life, from his sweet childhood photos to his wedding to Queen Sonja, his wife of almost 60 years. The young Harald was born on February 21, 1937 to the title of prince, being the third child and only son of then-Crown Prince Olav (later King Olav V) and Princess Märtha. He was the first prince born on Norwegian soil in 567 years. Here, he’s seen with his sisters older Princess Astrid and Princess Ragnhild. Harald came from a long royal legacy on both sides—his mother, Märtha, was the second daughter of Prince Carl of Sweden, son of King Oscar II. The royal family gathered for a sweet group portrait, including Princesses Ragnhild, Märtha, and Astrid, as well as little Prince Harald and his father Crown Prince Olav V. As one might expect, the future Norwegian king took to winter sports early. Here, he’s seen picking up some ski skills. This sweet photo shows young Harald enjoying an idyllic day playing on a swing. Following the German invasion of Norway in 1940, Harald, his mother, and sisters fled to the safety of the US. Here, Harald is seen at the beach on Cape Cod, where the royals lived on the estate of Pittsburgh socialite Frederic Schaefer. While his family stayed safe in America, Crown Prince Olav and his father, King Haakon VII, formed a government in exile in the U.K. However, in December 1940, the future monarch reunited with his wife and children in Bethesda, Maryland. While in North America, young Harald paid a visit to "Little Norway,” the Norwegian Air Force station in Canada, and even got to explore some of the aircraft. While they may not have been home for Christmas, Princess Astrid, Prince Harald and Princess Ragnhild still sent a radio Christmas greeting back to Norway. To mark his seventh birthday, Harald had this photo taken, showing the future king in his miniature military uniform. Harald and his family came to the US at the invitation of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, and they remained close with the American leader. Here, young Harald is seen playing with the president’s terrier, Fala, at FDR’s cousin Laura Delano's home in Rhinebeck, New York. With the end of WWII, the Norwegian royals were at last able to return home in 1945. For their landing at Oslo, they rode aboard the HSE Norfolk, and even borrowed some warmer coats from the crew to combat the chilly weather. The homecoming came with great fanfare, as people flooded the streets of Oslo to wave at Harald and his family in June 1945. As life began to return to normal, young Harald resumed school, where he was photographed 1946. The Norwegian royals remained close with their British cousins, traveling to the U.K. (in appropriately nautical style) to see the Olympic yachting events in 1948. Taken in 1949, this portrait shows the future king around age 12, and looking so grown up. Three generations of Norwegian royalty. Here, Harald joined his father Olav V, and grandfather King Haakon for a photo of the royal future. As is traditional for many royal family members, Harald attended the Norwegian Military Academy, entering the Cavalry Officers’s Training School. Here, he’s seen setting up his tent in  September 1956. Following the death of King Haakon the year before, Harald’s father, King Olav V held his official coronation on June 22, 1958. Naturally, Harald, the newly-minted Crown Prince, was at his side. title: Pope Leo mourns death of Norway’s King Harald V - Vatican News
content: King Harald V of Norway died at 6:35 a.m. on Friday at the Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet, after being taken to the national hospital last week to treat a serious blood disorder. Harald V reigned for more than 35 years, making him the longest-reigning Norwegian monarch since King Haakon VII. The late King's son, Crown Prince Haakon, has succeeded him as King Haakon VIII. Hours after the monarch's death, Pope Leo sent a telegram to offer his condolences to King Haakon VIII for the death of his father. The Pope said he was saddened to learn of the death of King Harald and sent "heartfelt condolences" to the new King, the members of the royal family and all the people of Norway. "Mindful of his many years of devoted service to the realm, which I hope will continue to bear fruit," Pope Leo said, "I offer the assurance of my prayers for the eternal rest of the late King." Finally, the Holy Father cordially invoked God’s blessings of consolation and peace upon the Norwegian people and all who mourn his loss. Bishop Eric Varden of Trondheim and Apostolic Administrator of Tromsø likewise expressed his condolences, saying that today Harald V made this passage from physical death to life, saying that with "reverence and gratitude we commend him to God’s loving mercy." The Bishop said that King Harald "embodied the nation" in an "exemplary manner." "We were aware that he saw us, knew us, valued us," he said, adding, "We knew his care, were embraced by the warmth he exuded. He gave us a magnificent example of dedication." Bishop Varden stressed that Harald "was so entirely our king, given to his people. No ego seemed to stand in the way. That brought him near to us in a wholly beneficent way." Finally, the Bishop concluded by reassuring that the Catholics of Norway pray for the late King, the royal family, and the new King. Thank you for reading our article. title: Norway’s King Harald V dies, succeeded by son - Al Jazeera
content: Harald V, who was Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, has died at the age of 89. His son will reign as King Haakon VIII. Norway’s King Harald V has died at the age of 89, after being hospitalised with a rare blood condition. The death of Europe’s oldest reigning monarch was announced on Friday by the Royal Palace of Norway. “King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, Aug 28 at 6:35 a.m,” the palace said in a statement. His son, Crown Prince Haakon, automatically succeeds him and is expected to reign as King Haakon VIII. Royal family members had visited the king on Thursday, and crowds gathered outside the palace and laid flowers for the king after officials warned that his condition had turned “extremely serious”. Harald was hospitalised on August 17, suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne 35 years ago, has had multiple health problems in recent years, forcing him to have a pacemaker fitted and to scale back his official schedule. But he had always ruled out abdicating, arguing that he took a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament. Harald was Norway’s first king born on Norwegian soil since the 14th century. Taking the throne in January 1991, after the death of his father, Olav V, he presided over decades of oil-fuelled prosperity. He was born in February 1937, near Oslo. When the Nazis invaded Norway his mother fled with him and his sisters to Sweden and then the United States, while his father and grandfather, Haakon VII, sat out the war in Britain. Harald won lasting public affection for his speech in 2011 after Anders Behring Breivik‘s bomb attacks which killed 77 people, telling mourners: “I remain convinced that the belief in freedom is stronger than fear.” His death, however, comes at a fraught time for the monarchy, after documents published in January showed Crown Princess Mette-Marit corresponding with notorious US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, years after his conviction. Her 29-year-old son, Marius Borg Høiby, the new King Haakon’s stepson, was sentenced in June to four years in prison on two counts of rape and 32 other charges, including domestic violence.

title: Bishop prays for Norway’s King Harald V, hails ‘stable pillar’ - EWTN News
content: Bishop Erik Varden invoked a ninth-century prayer for the dying as he commended King Harald V to God’s mercy on behalf of Norwegian Catholics. King Harald V of Norway, Europeʼs oldest reigning monarch, died on Aug. 28 at Oslo University Hospital. He was 89. A Requiem Mass for King Harald will be celebrated at St. Olavʼs Cathedral in Trondheim on Aug. 29 at noon, and lauds and vespers will also be offered for the late monarch. EWTN Norway is streaming the services on its website and YouTube channel. Within hours of the kingʼs death, Bishop Erik Varden of Trondheim published a tribute on behalf of Norwegian Catholics. He commended Harald to Godʼs mercy and offered prayers for Queen Sonja, the royal family, and the new King Haakon VIII. Varden, a Trappist monk who also serves as apostolic administrator of Tromsø and president of the Nordic Bishops' Conference, opened his reflection with the ninth-century “Commendatio Animae” — the Churchʼs prayer for the dying. “Go forth, Christian soul, from this world in the name of God, the Almighty Father, who created you; in the name of Jesus Christ, the living Son of God, who suffered for you; and in the name of the Holy Spirit, who was poured out upon you,” the prayer begins. Varden wrote that the prayer reminds the faithful that death is a transition “from life to Life.” Varden described Harald as a monarch who embodied the nation in an exemplary way, giving Norwegians a sense of being seen and cared for. “He was so completely and utterly king, devoted to the people, that it was as if no ego stood in the way,” the bishop wrote. “In this way, he drew near to us in a comforting way.” Harald “has spoken wisely to us, with a subtle sense of humor that we will miss,” Varden added. The bishop placed the kingʼs passing in the context of the ancient acclamation “The King is dead; long live the King,” and wrote that the monarchy stands as “a stable pillar in society” that represents continuity. “In a time as uncertain as ours, that is a comfort,” he wrote. Varden called on Norwegian Catholics to pray for King Haakon VIII. He asked the faithful for “blessings and wisdom” and called on Catholics to stand loyally by the new sovereign. Closing his tribute, the bishop invoked the intercession of St. Olav, Norwayʼs patron saint. Harald V was born on Feb. 21, 1937, and ascended the throne on Jan. 17, 1991, succeeding his father, King Olav V. He reigned for 35 years. A three-time Olympic yachtsman, Harald modernized the Norwegian royal house. Later in his life, he refused to abdicate, saying he had taken a lifelong oath before the Norwegian Parliament. He had experienced multiple health problems in recent years. Harald is survived by Queen Sonja, 89, his wife of 57 years, and their two children: Princess Märtha Louise, 54, and the new King Haakon VIII, 53. His granddaughter, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, is now next in line to the throne. This report draws on coverage by EWTN Norway and reporting by Pål Johannes Nes. title: Norway's King Harald V dies at 89, his son becomes King Haakon VIII - France 24
content: King Harald V of Norway, who was Europe's oldest reigning monarch, died at the age of 89, the palace announced on Friday. He is automatically succeeded by his son, King Haakon VIII, the former crown prince. King Harald V of Norway, has died at the age of 89, according to an announcement by the palace Friday morning. Harald was Europe’s oldest monarch. As a child, he went into exile in the United States as a child during the Nazi occupation of his homeland and became known for refusing a string of European noblewomen in order to marry his school sweetheart. The popular king modernised the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other royals who had chosen to  abdicate in old age. His son, the former crown prince automatically succeeds him as King Haakon VIII. Like other royal houses in Europe, the Norwegian monarchs serve a largely symbolic role, enjoying celebrity status while real power in the democratic nation of 5.5 million rests with an elected parliament. Harald was crowned king after his British-born father, King Olav V, died in January 1991, and reigned during Norway's an oil-and-gas-driven economic boom, which commenced in the late 1960s. Harald was born in 1937 in Asker, near Oslo, becoming the first Norwegian prince to be born in the country since King Olav IV in 1370. In the following centuries, Norway didn't have a king of its own until Harald's grandfather, Haakon VII, was appointed in the aftermath of the 1905 dissolution of the union between Sweden and Norway. He was 3 years old when the Nazis occupied Norway at the start of World War II. To avoid capture, his mother fled with him and his sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid – first to Sweden and then by boat to the US, while Harald’s father and grandfather went into exile in Britain with the aide of Norway’s government. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site. Haakon’s refusal to go along with German demands garnered respect among his people. During their time in the US, the Norwegian royals were often guests at the White House. Harald was 6 years old when he carried out his first official duty, christening new warplanes at a Norwegian air base in Canada. The family was reunited in Norway in June 1945, shortly after the end of the war. He attended public schools, the Norwegian military college and Oxford University. Like his father – an Olympic champion sailor in 1928 – Harald loved the sea and sailboats. He represented Norway at several Olympics, and in 1987 he skippered his yacht to gold in the World Championships. As a young man, Harald was urged to find a bride among the princesses of Europe. For nine years he shunned a series of noblewomen, holding out until he finally won his father’s permission to marry his school sweetheart, Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a successful businessman. King Olav had feared the marriage would weaken Norway’s still-young monarchy. Instead, Norwegians greeted the pair's wedding on August 29, 1968 with jubilation, later embracing Sonja as their queen. The couple had two children, Haakon and his older sister, Märtha Louise. The Norwegian Constitution was altered in 1990 to allow the first born – regardless of gender – to take precedence in the line of succession. However, it was not applied retroactively, meaning that Haakon's future as reigning monarch was set, over that of his sister. When Harald assumed the throne on January 21, 1991, he adopted the same motto as his father and grandfather: “All for Norway.” He spent the next years trying to modernise the monarchy. “It has been my experience that the monarchy stands strong,” he once said. “This is not least because my father and grandfather did most things right. That puts me under pressure, but I take it as a challenge.” Harald won the praise of the country with an emotional speech at a memorial service after a right-wing extremist, Anders Behring Breivik, killed 77 people in bomb and gun attacks in Norway in 2011. “I remain convinced that the belief in freedom is stronger than fear. I remain convinced in the belief of an open Norwegian democracy and society. I remain convinced in the belief in our ability to live freely and safely in our own country," the king said. In 2016, Harald gave an unexpected and impassioned speech in support of LGBTQ+ equality, refugees and religious tolerance, saying “Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other.” He added that many Norwegians had emigrated from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Poland and other countries and that they “believe in God, Allah, the universe and nothing.” The public speech extolled the diversity of the Scandinavian nation and was viewed on social media by millions. Read moreSon of Norway's crown princess sentenced to four years in prison for rape During his reign, the royal family suffered relatively few of the scandals that have plagued their peers in the Swedish and British royal families, though Harald's daughter Märtha Louise gave up royal duties after raising eyebrows by saying she could communicate with angels and becoming engaged to an American man who identifies as a shaman. The Norwegian royal family faced unflattering attention in early 2026 as Harald’s daughter-in-law, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, was scrutinised for connections with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Her association with him raised questions over her judgment, though she is not accused of any wrongdoing. Mette-Marit subsequently apologised for the situation she put the royal family in, as part of a broader apology for all those she had “disappointed.” At around the same time, Mette-Marie's eldest son, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted of rape in a high-profile trial and sentenced to four years in prison. Høiby is her son from a previous relationship before she had met Haakon. He has no royal titles or official duties. In January 2024, after the abdication of Denmark’s Queen Margrethe – who is Harald's second cousin – the late king said he stood by the oath he made when ascending the throne: “It lasts for life”. However, following this he was hospitalised twice on foreign trips, including during a 2024 break in Malaysia, where he was fitted with a pacemaker, and in February 2026 while dealing with a skin infection during a holiday to the Spanish island of Tenerife. © 2026 Copyright France 24 - All rights reserved. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, August 28 at 6:35 am," it said in a statement. The flag at the royal palace in Oslo was lowered to half-mast on Friday as members of the public gathered outside to lay flowers and pay tribute to King Harald. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered her condolences to the Norwegian people, describing Harald as a "true European" who had served his country "with warmth, humility and an unwavering sense of duty". "In moments of joy and sorrow, he brought Norwegians together," she said, adding that his royal motto, "Alt for Norge" meaning "All for Norway," would continue to resonate. French President Emmanuel Macron expressed "deep sadness", hailing the monarch's contribution to diplomacy saying the late king "worked tirelessly throughout his reign to strengthen the ties uniting Norway and France." Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf said "both as head of state and a successful athlete, he was an outstanding representative of his country. He gave 'All for Norway'." Denmark's King Frederik said the late monarch was "an extraordinary man" who "joined duty and responsibility with presence and compassion". The 89-year-old had been in hospital since August 17 with haemolytic anaemia, a condition in which red blood cells are destroyed faster than they can be replaced. His family rushed to his bedside on Thursday after the palace announced that his condition had become "extremely serious", with Crown Prince Haakon reportedly keeping vigil overnight. Harald, who ascended the throne in 1991, had suffered several health problems in recent years and had a pacemaker fitted, but repeatedly ruled out abdicating because of the lifelong oath he took before parliament. Mourners described him as a warm and inclusive monarch who had helped unite Norway, while Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre cancelled a planned trip to Germany as the king's condition deteriorated. King Harald V remained a popular and unifying figure throughout his 35-year reign, helping modernise Norway's monarchy while steering it through moments of national tragedy and, in his final years, family scandal. For centuries, Norway shared monarchs with Denmark and later Sweden, meaning its royal families were largely based outside the country. That changed after Norway became fully independent in 1905, and Harald's birth near Oslo in 1937 made him the first Norwegian-born prince in more than 500 years. He was three when Nazi Germany invaded in 1940 and fled with his mother and sisters to Sweden and then the United States, while his father and grandfather went into exile in Britain. The family returned to Norway after the war in 1945. Harald attended public schools, trained at Norway's military academy and studied at the University of Oxford. A talented sailor, he represented Norway at three Olympic Games and later won a world championship. He married Sonja Haraldsen, his childhood sweetheart, in 1968 after a nine-year period to win his father's approval. The couple had two children, Märtha Louise and Haakon. Harald succeeded his father, King Olav V, in 1991, adopting the royal motto "All for Norway". Despite having limited constitutional powers, he became known for his ability to unite the country at difficult moments. After Anders Behring Breivik killed 77 people in 2011, Harald declared that "freedom is stronger than fear". He also championed an increasingly diverse Norway, winning widespread praise for a 2016 speech embracing LGBTQ+ people, immigrants and different religious beliefs. His oratory was about inclusion and national unity in which he said "Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other." The king also supported immigrants and people of different faiths, before saying: "Norway is you. Norway is us."
